item.title: The statistical analysis of complete compositional data
item.description: arXiv:2611.28157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The analysis of compositional data is dominated by the use of Aitchison's logratio transformation; which is the logarithmic transformation of ratios of compositional features. The use of ratios was originally justified to comply with the principle of subcompositional coherence.However, there are many situations in practice where the complete composition is observed, that is, the totality of its mutually exclusive features, without the need for considering any subcompositions. In these cases, the data can be analysed on the original compositional scale, which provides a simpler and often more valid interpretation than logratios. Two real examples of complete compositional data are considered and the properties of alternative approaches to analysing them are compared. These ideas extend to some cases of incomplete compositions, where analysing them at their original scale, or normalized according to domain knowledge, is more appropriate. A Supplement includes a detailed comparison of original-scale and logratio-transformed 24-hour activity data, using a data set typical of many found in the time-use literature.
item.dc:creator: Michael Greenacre, Ionas Erb

item.title: Conditional Independence Testing for Random Objects via Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.28222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a test of conditional independence for random objects taking values in metric spaces of negative type, allowing the conditioning variable to be either a random object or a high-dimensional vector. Our method uses multidimensional scaling and Nystr\"om extensions to obtain finite-dimensional representations of random objects from their pairwise distances, and generative neural networks to estimate conditional distributions in the embedded space. Samples from the fitted generators are then used to construct a doubly robust test statistic. Our main theoretical contribution is to quantify how errors from estimating and truncating the embeddings, together with errors in learning the conditional distributions, affect inference. We establish conditions under which these errors are asymptotically negligible, even when the embedding dimensions grow with the sample size. In particular, we derive explicit convergence rates when the conditional distributions admit generators with smooth, low-dimensional compositional structure. We establish asymptotic validity of the bootstrap test, consistency against fixed alternatives, and nontrivial power against local alternatives. Simulations with distribution-valued data demonstrate its competitive finite-sample performance.
item.dc:creator: Yi Zhang, Yun Yang, Xiaofeng Shao

item.title: Threshold Generalized Autoregressive Moving Average Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.28271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Gaussian time series often exhibit nonlinear dynamics and changes in dependence structures that may not be adequately captured by conventional single-regime models. To address this limitation, we introduce a class of threshold generalized autoregressive moving-average (TGARMA) models that combines observation-driven GARMA dynamics with threshold-based regime switching. The proposed framework accommodates multiple regimes, determined by a lagged endogenous or exogenous threshold variable, and allows regression coefficients, autoregressive and moving-average orders and coefficients, and, where applicable, dispersion parameters to vary across regimes. Parameters are estimated by maximum partial likelihood, while model selection is conducted using information criteria. We examine model admissibility and stability, assess model adequacy through residual diagnostics, and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to investigate the finite-sample performance of the estimators. The proposed methodology is illustrated using monthly counts of hospitalizations due to respiratory diseases among older adults in S\~ao Paulo, Brazil. In this application, the TGARMA model outperforms its single-regime GARMA counterpart in terms of in-sample mean squared error, highlighting the potential benefits of incorporating regime-dependent dynamics into the analysis of non-Gaussian time series.
item.dc:creator: Katerine Zuniga Lastra, Airlane Pereira Alencar

item.title: Skew-Symmetric Factor Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.28301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The paper introduces and analyzes a factor model for (real) skew-symmetric data, which arise naturally in directed flows and in pairwise comparisons used for rankings. Working within a signal-plus-noise framework, we analyze spectral inference and establish a BBP-type phase transition in signal strength. Under Gaussian noise, we derive joint eigenvalue fluctuation limits. Above the separation threshold, the estimated signal strength is asymptotically normal whenever the population strength has multiplicity one. For a general multiplicity $k$, the joint limiting fluctuations of the corresponding sample eigenvalues above the threshold are given by the eigenvalues of a scaled $k\times k$ Gaussian unitary ensemble matrix. The skew-symmetric structure induces paired eigenspaces, and we characterize the canonical angles between the population and sample eigenspaces. Below the threshold, the corresponding largest sample eigenvalue converges to the edge of the semicircle law, with fluctuations governed by the Tracy--Widom $F_2$ distribution, in contrast to the $F_1$ law familiar from real symmetric models. The approach is illustrated through financial and demographic applications.
item.dc:creator: Anna Bykhovskaya, Tomas Espana, Jianqing Fan

item.title: Treatment Policy Design in the Presence of Measurement Error
item.description: arXiv:2611.28372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many applications, treatments are assigned based on unit features, leading to personalized treatment policies. This often involves optimizing objective functions with counterfactual quantities such as the conditional average treatment effect (CATE). In practice, some key features may be measured with error and ignoring such errors can introduce systematic bias. We study how to design personalized treatment policies when some features are latent and only noisy measurements are available. We ask how policies can be constructed when the CATE is not identifiable, and how uncertainty from measurement error can be incorporated into policy design. We propose two frameworks for treatment policy design based on partial identification, focusing on the measurement mechanism-the conditional distribution of observed measurements given unobserved features. The first framework builds on ideas from proximal causal inference. The second adopts a modular Bayesian approach based on a reparameterized likelihood, using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Bayesian regression models to separately perform posterior inference on the measurement mechanism and nuisance functions. Posterior quantiles are then used to construct credible intervals for the CATE that account for uncertainty in both components. Treatment policies are then derived by comparing the null value of the CATE to these bounds. The proposed methods provide a coherent way to account for measurement error and model uncertainty in personalized treatment policy design.
item.dc:creator: Chang Liu, AmirEmad Ghassami

item.title: Statistical inference under response-adaptive experimental designs: a systematic review
item.description: arXiv:2611.28380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Response-adaptive designs, including bandit-based approaches, update treatment allocation using accrued outcomes. In this paper, we systematically reviewed how studies in health and biostatistics conducted and evaluated inference under these designs. We searched six databases for studies published from January 2010 through October 2025. Of 774 records identified, 36 studies met the inclusion criteria. We summarized them using study-level counts and structured narrative comparisons, with reporting guided by PRISMA 2020. Most studies focused on methods or designs. Evidence supporting inference came mainly from theory and simulation. Among studies for which each metric was relevant, 26 of 32 numerically evaluated power, 23 of 32 type I error, eight of 35 estimator bias, and five of 12 interval coverage. These findings suggest that studies more often quantified power and type I error than estimator bias or interval coverage. Evaluations of adaptive allocation should also examine estimation and interval performance when these are relevant to the study objective.
item.dc:creator: Haochen Song, Joseph Williams, Kiarash Kianidehkordi, Audrey Durand, Anna Rafferty, Tong Li, Meredith Franklin

item.title: A Bayesian Mechanistic Model of Spatiotemporal Dynamics in Invasive Tree Species
item.description: arXiv:2611.28432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modeling the spatiotemporal dynamics of invasive species requires frameworks that represent spread and growth mechanisms explicitly while accommodating the distributional features of ecological data. We propose a Bayesian mechanistic framework for invasive tree cover that combines an ecological diffusion--logistic growth partial differential equation (PDE) with a zero-inflated binomial observation model. The diffusion and growth coefficients are modeled as functions of environmental covariates, enabling direct inference on the ecological processes driving encroachment, and the zero-inflation component separates structural absence from low observed cover. To enable scalable Bayesian inference on satellite-resolution grids, we derive a homogenized equation for ecological diffusion with spatially varying diffusion and growth coefficients, which reduces computation while preserving large-scale spatial structure. Applied to satellite-derived tree cover in a subregion of the Nebraska Sandhills, where eastern redcedar is encroaching on grassland, the model indicates that elevation is strongly associated with where tree cover accumulates but only weakly with its local growth rate, whereas distance to the nearest stream is associated with both. Compared with a generalized additive model, a spatial hierarchical model fitted via INLA, and a regression tree, the proposed method directly estimates these processes as interpretable functions of environmental covariates and gives the best-calibrated predictive uncertainty.
item.dc:creator: Jiaqi Chen, Huijing Du, Yawen Guan

item.title: When AI Performance Is Not Enough: Statistical Guardrails for Clinical Development
item.description: arXiv:2611.28497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are reshaping the operational and inferential landscape of clinical development, yet their adoption frequently outpaces the statistical scrutiny these methods demand. This commentary offers first-principles perspectives across four application domains: anomaly detection in clinical trial data, real-time monitoring and adaptive trial designs, biomarker-based enrichment, and virtual and digital twins. For each domain, we articulate the underlying inferential problem, the contribution of AI and ML relative to established statistical methods, and the risks that statisticians, data scientists, and clinical developers must actively manage. Across these domains, a unifying theme emerges: AI and ML methods may succeed locally while failing to satisfy the broader statistical assumptions required for valid clinical and regulatory decisions. These risks include false-positive signals, compromised Type I error control in adaptive designs, conflation of prognostic with predictive biomarkers, and causal claims not supported by data and assumptions. We argue that a clearly defined context of use, relevant statistical assumptions, and consequences of the intended decision should guide the evaluation. For treatment-effect questions, the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework provides a useful organizing principle. Responsible use of AI in clinical development requires not restraint, but rigor: the inferential discipline necessary to make these technologies reproducible, interpretable, and defensible in the service of patients.
item.dc:creator: Siddhesh Kulkarni, Gina D'Angelo, Swarna Reddy, Rakhi Kilaru

item.title: LEAF: Calibrated and Robust Wavelet Estimation of the Hurst Exponent
item.description: arXiv:2611.28538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wavelet logscale regression for the Hurst exponent H of fractional Brownian motion (fBm) is sensitive to outliers and biased in finite samples. We introduce the Log-Energy with Adaptive Floor (LEAF) ordinate, which averages the logarithms of squared wavelet coefficients after adding a floor proportional to a pilot estimate of the level variance. If standardized coefficients share a common law across levels, a floor proportional to the true level variance preserves the population slope, and a consistent pilot preserves it asymptotically. We derive the asymptotic variance and influence function, and identify the variance-minimizing floor for median-pilot LEAF, whose influence grows only logarithmically. With outliers of ten increment standard deviations in up to 1% of observations, median-pilot LEAF reduces root mean squared error by a factor of 1.8 to 2.6 relative to calibrated log-energy. At H = 0.5 with 1% outliers, the error falls from 0.139 to 0.059. For small to moderate H, the main source of bias is the departure of expected wavelet energies from the ideal power law at fine scales. We estimate H from an estimating equation calibrated by simulation under fBm. Calibrating the mean logscale diagram alone delivers nearly all of the gain: it nearly eliminates bias in matched simulations and improves on the Abry--Veitch estimator most at small H. Simulations also show how scale-dependent tails can erode the gains of a robust pilot and how misspecification can undermine calibration.
item.dc:creator: Vijini Lakmini, Brani Vidakovic

item.title: The Curved Exponential Family of Cylindrical Distributions: m-Projection, Curvature and a Test of the von Mises-Fisher Component
item.description: arXiv:2611.28598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cylindrical data pair a vector in R^d with a direction in S^(m-1). We study a family in which the direction is von Mises-Fisher and, given the direction, the vector is Gaussian with mean affine in it; this generalizes the Mardia-Sutton model. The family is a curved exponential family inside a regular family with Fisher-Bingham directions. We state necessary and sufficient conditions for the maximum-likelihood estimator to exist and be unique. The estimator is explicit except for one scalar root and is the m-projection (Kullback-Leibler projection) of the moment-matching member. Every moment it does not match is a function of one residual, the gap between the sample and fitted second moments of the direction. The squared length of this gap in the Fisher metric is the classical score test of von Mises-Fisher against Fisher-Bingham directions, due to Cox on the circle and extended by Mardia, Holmes and Kent. Specific here are this reading and the exact invariance of its law to the regression part. The exponential curvature lies only in the directions of the regression matrix. In closed form, the information lost on this matrix against the expected information is m-1 observations for uniform directions and (m+1)^2/(m-1) in the limit of high concentration; conditioning on the directions recovers it. Finite mixtures are identifiable. On buoy records the test rejects von Mises-Fisher directions, and generalized von Mises directions raise the held-out log-density by 0.45 nats per observation with one component.
item.dc:creator: Amine M. Aboussalah

item.title: Robust Forest-based Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Under High-dimensional Confounding
item.description: arXiv:2611.28662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how patients with Alzheimer's disease respond differently to treatment is important for individualized therapeutic assessment. Using observational data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we investigate how the association between donepezil dosage and 12-month cognitive performance varies across diagnostic stages and hippocampal volumes. This analysis presents several statistical challenges, including potentially nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity, high-dimensional confounding, and heavy-tailed outcomes with extreme observations. To address these challenges, we develop an Orthogonal Huber Random Forest (OHRF) framework that combines Huber-based robust estimation, Neyman orthogonality, and forest-based adaptive weighting. The proposed method accommodates complex treatment effect heterogeneity while reducing sensitivity to nuisance estimation errors and extreme outcomes. We establish its consistency, asymptotic normality, and finite-sample error bounds. Simulation studies demonstrate favorable estimation accuracy and robustness across a range of error distributions, particularly under heavy-tailed noise and outlier contamination. In the ADNI application, OHRF produces generally narrower pointwise confidence intervals than the conventional Orthogonal Random Forest (ORF) while revealing distinct patterns of treatment effect heterogeneity across diagnostic groups and hippocampal volumes. These findings illustrate the potential of robust, data-adaptive methods for studying heterogeneous treatment responses in complex observational biomedical data.
item.dc:creator: Zhixin Qiu, Xuanxuan Wang, Xinyuan Song, Yinfeng Wang, Yanlin Tang

item.title: Cure-Fraction Random Survival Forests: Separating Cure from Latency
item.description: arXiv:2611.28770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many cancer and clinical studies, the population under study has a positive fraction of long-term survivors, motivating survival models that distinguish probability of long-term survival (cure fraction) from the latency of the subgroup that is susceptible to the event. Existing survival trees and forests partition data using criteria that emphasize differences in the ranks of survival times and therefore need not identify covariates associated with cure probability. We introduce cure-fraction based survival trees (CBST) that recursively partition the covariate space using contrasts in tail survival probability supported by adequate follow-up. The resulting ensemble forest targets long-term survival heterogeneity directly rather than ranking of the survival times. We establish consistency for the induced tail-survival target and derive conditions under which our procedure consistently recovers cure-rate related partitions and cure probabilities. The analysis clarifies the separate roles of follow-up maturity, localization, and residual-tail bias in identifying cure effects and supporting statistical inference. We further develop variance estimation and asymptotic results and uncertainty quantification for predictions from the ensemble forest. Simulations show that the cure-fraction based splitting criterion can improve recovery of cure heterogeneity relative to a log-rank based forest when cure incidence and latency are driven by different covariates. Analyses of temporally held-out cohorts from the Sao Paulo Hospital Cancer Registry demonstrate that our method produces stable long-term survival risk groups while preserving substantial late follow-up support. The proposed framework provides a nonparametric approach to learning and interpreting cure heterogeneity in settings where long-term survival is the primary scientific objective.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Luiz Ramos, Lucas Osses, Debajyoti Sinha

item.title: Censored Regression Models with Endogeneity: A Survey
item.description: arXiv:2611.28835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This survey article provides a comprehensive overview of methodologies developed to handle endogeneity in censored regression models. We emphasize their theoretical basis, and estimating methodologies. The paper summarizes the benefits and drawbacks of each technique and addresses expansions to nonlinear, panel, and high-dimensional settings, offering researchers practical assistance and identifying options for future methodological improvement in censored models with endogenous regressors.
item.dc:creator: Swati Shukla, Shalabh, Subhra Sankar Dhar

item.title: Twisted Block Particle Filters: A Local Particle-System Change of Measure for High-Dimensional State-Space Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.28848v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Block particle filters mitigate weight degeneracy in high-dimensional state-space models, but their normalizer estimates can remain highly variable. We introduce a twisted block particle filter (TBPF) that incorporates predictive guidance through an exact change of measure at blockwise resampling. The method guide-tilts one uniformly selected offspring per block, leaves the state-transition kernel unchanged, and computes the resampling correction using finite empirical guide averages. We prove that this correction exactly preserves the finite-particle block particle filter normalizer expectation, separating the effect of guided sampling from the approximation introduced by spatial blocking. Our analysis provides exact conditional local moments and a one-step conditional central limit result. We further derive explicit bounds on the correction accumulated across blocks and time, establish fixed-horizon consistency of the block filter and corrected normalizer under suitable regularity and guide-range conditions, and identify conditional criteria for guide perturbations that reduce variance. Experiments on coupled linear Gaussian and stochastic-volatility models with up to 256 latent dimensions show lower measured log-normalizer variance. For stochastic volatility with a five-step guide, the median reduction is $38\%$. An application to a 100-dimensional financial portfolio panel extends the evaluation to real data.
item.dc:creator: Ning Ning

item.title: Correlation-aware sequential sampling for multi-output polynomial chaos expansions
item.description: arXiv:2611.28877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The interaction of multiple physical processes in complex engineering systems is often characterized by several quantities of interest (QoIs) with non-negligible cross-correlations. Accurate uncertainty quantification of these responses requires repeated model evaluations, which can be computationally expensive. As an alternative, polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) provides an efficient surrogate modeling framework for reducing this computational cost owing to its natural structure for statistical analysis, while adaptive sequential sampling can further improve sampling efficiency under a limited model evaluation budget. However, adaptive sampling strategies specifically designed for multi-output PCE remain limited, and existing approaches commonly aggregate information from individual outputs without explicitly accounting for their statistical dependence. When strong correlations exist among QoIs, output-wise aggregation can give greater combined influence to response patterns shared by several outputs. To reduce the influence of such repeated representation on sample allocation, this study develops a principal component analysis-based extension of the multi-output criterion for adaptive construction of PCE. The sampling criterion combines component-wise normalization with the retention of selected principal directions, thereby adjusting the relative influence of shared response patterns while preserving distance-based exploration. The method is verified through numerical examples with different levels of output coupling and is compared with the conventional multi-output criterion and reference sampling strategies. The results demonstrate that accounting for output dependence improves the allocation of new samples among multiple response features and enhances the efficiency of multi-output PCE surrogate construction, particularly for strongly correlated QoIs.
item.dc:creator: Qitian Lu, Miroslav Vo\v{r}echovsk\'y, Luk\'a\v{s} Nov\'ak

item.title: Adaptive Two-Sample Testing for Regression Discrepancy and Model Misspecification in High Dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2611.28892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In two-sample regression comparisons, testing for equality is often too restrictive because minor discrepancies in functional form are unavoidable in practice. We study whether the functional discrepancy falls within a practically acceptable tolerance. Such tolerance-based comparison can, however, be unreliable when either regression model is misspecified. To address both issues, we propose a unified adaptive-to-model testing framework for high-dimensional regressions that integrates model checking with functional similarity testing for the two populations. For functional similarity, we develop an adaptive boundary-proxy test whose rejection probability converges to the nominal level at every fixed configuration of the composite null hypothesis, overcoming the conservatism of conventional least favorable configuration tests. For model misspecification, we use projection-based tests for sparse high-dimensional regression models. These components are combined through adaptive gating into a joint test. We investigate its asymptotic null distribution and power properties under global and local alternatives. Numerical studies examine its finite-sample performance.
item.dc:creator: Yu Peng, Jiaqi Huang, Falong Tan, Lixing Zhu

item.title: ATLAS: Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival
item.description: arXiv:2611.29152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic survival prediction requires estimates that reflect a patient's observed clinical history. We introduce ATLAS (Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival), a framework that trains a sequence model on longitudinal data and autoregressively samples possible futures conditional on an individual's covariates and observed history. These trajectories form a patient-specific synthetic cohort from which Kaplan-Meier survival curves and Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence curves are estimated. We evaluate ATLAS using two stochastic finite-state automaton benchmarks with exact conditional reference curves: a single-covariate process with duration dependence and a late rule change, and a three-covariate Markov process with recovery and competing causes of death. Comparisons include eight direct survival models, including validation-optimized DRSA and Dynamic-DeepHit and history-aware SurvTRACE adaptations, with each neural model trained nine times in the first experiment and five times in the second. After baseline, every ATLAS configuration had lower mean survival-curve error than every fitted direct comparator in both experiments. With a common Sobol sampler and 10,000 trajectories per patient, the best ATLAS model did so in every individual training run, and its mean error was 62% to 84% lower than that of the strongest direct comparator. Baseline advantages were smaller and less consistent in the duration-dependent experiment. ATLAS provides a generative framework for history-conditioned survival estimation, while the accompanying benchmarks enable direct assessment of individual survival and competing-risk predictions against known reference curves.
item.dc:creator: Morgan Nissen, Chunyang Li, Seth Glazier, Julia Bohman, Ahmad Halwani, Jeffrey Humpherys

item.title: Model Selection and Averaging: Signal Strength, Ordering, and Oracle Risks
item.description: arXiv:2611.29189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing oracle risk comparisons of model selection (MS) and model averaging (MA) have primarily distinguished slowly and rapidly decaying ordered signal-importance sequences, leaving the comparison beyond these idealized but practically unrepresentative decay conditions insufficiently characterized. We revisit this problem for a complete nested collection of linear regression models with independent homoscedastic errors. Without prescribing a coefficient decay pattern, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the relative oracle gain of MA over MS to be asymptotically substantial or negligible. Under complete ordering of the coefficients, the determining quantity is the share of oracle MS risk contributed by components near the noise level. This characterization explains how the strengths and numbers of strong, moderate, and weak signals jointly affect the comparison. Under an arbitrary fixed ordering, a common pool-adjacent-violators partition represents both oracle risks and yields an analogous characterization through block averages and sizes. For application, we develop a consistent diagnostic under sub-Gaussian errors and suitable growth conditions, together with finite-sample confidence intervals under Gaussian errors. The Gaussian framework also provides confidence sets for a certain Rashomon set. Simulations and a diamond-price application illustrate the theoretical findings and the empirical assessment of the potential MA advantage.
item.dc:creator: Guangyuan Cui, Yuhong Yang

item.title: Why flattening the P-value histogram works: a theory of the standard-deviation optimization in tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction
item.description: arXiv:2611.29201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: Tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction (TD-based UFE) selects genes by attributing P-values to the components of a gene singular vector under a null normal distribution. The standard deviation sigma of this distribution is unknown and is chosen so that the histogram of the P-values of the genes that are not selected becomes as flat as possible. This heuristic has worked well in practice but has had no theoretical justification. Results: We prove, for a model of signal, mean expression and noise, that the higher-order singular value decomposition has a component that reproduces the experimental design, that the components of its gene singular vector belonging to background genes are approximately normal with standard deviation sigma_0 = sqrt(d)/s, where d is the noise variance and s the singular value, and that signal genes separate from the background even when they form a positive fraction of all genes. We derive the limit of the objective function of the flattening and prove, by a computer-assisted argument based on interval arithmetic, that for 100 histogram bins, Benjamini-Hochberg level 0.01 and every fraction of background genes between 0.1 and 0.99, the limit has a unique minimizer within 1.1% of sigma_0. We formalize the practice of taking the valley to the right of the peak of the objective as a maximum-drop rule and prove that the resulting estimator is consistent up to this bounded bias. Conclusions: Flattening the P-value histogram estimates the noise level of the background genes, with a small and bounded systematic bias, provided that the signals are strong enough to be detected individually and that the noise variances of background genes are nearly equal.
item.dc:creator: Y-h. Taguchi, Turki Turki

item.title: Deep Negative Binomial Autoregression for Sparse Spatio-Temporal Counts: Estimation and Predictive Distribution Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2611.29207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study estimation and probabilistic forecasting for sparse, overdispersed count panels using DeepNB-STAR, a negative binomial autoregression whose log-mean and log-size are outputs of a deep ReLU network of temporal and neighboring summaries of the past, fitted by maximum likelihood. We prove an oracle inequality for the Hellinger risk along the observed trajectory without mixing assumptions, rates governed by compositional smoothness with a matching lower bound for a H\"older subclass, geometric absolute regularity, and bounds on the error of h-step predictive distributions of order h^{1/2} times the root estimation risk plus a Monte Carlo term. All results hold for a size that depends on the covariates, and the estimation bounds hold under arbitrary dependence between sites, with the number of time points as sample size. On four Japanese surveillance panels, DeepNB-STAR has a weighted interval score 0.6% to 1.0% below that of a three-member ensemble of Temporal Fusion Transformers on every panel, distinguishable from zero only on the held-out panel. Fitted mean and size functions are reported with exploratory bootstrap intervals. Nominal 95% prediction intervals for national totals cover only 81% to 92% of weeks: the joint predictive law, unlike the estimator, relies on conditional independence across sites.
item.dc:creator: Hsin-Hsiung Huang

item.title: Checking the Cumulative Exposure Model: Cumulative Chi-Squared Goodness-of-Fit Tests for Interval-Monitored Step-Stress Life Tests
item.description: arXiv:2611.29374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In an interval-monitored step-stress life test the data are the numbers of devices that fail between consecutive inspections. These cells are ordered in time, but the usual goodness-of-fit check, Pearson's statistic, ignores the order. We propose goodness-of-fit tests based on the cumulative residuals, the differences between the empirical and the fitted distribution functions at the inspection times, with the parameters estimated by the minimum density power divergence estimator. The two statistics are Taguchi's cumulative chi-squared statistic and its version with constant weights, the classical members of a family of cumulative divergences for ordered categories, with the null probabilities replaced by those of the fitted model. For the exponential cumulative exposure model with a log-linear link we prove the existence, uniqueness and consistency of the estimator under explicit conditions, and we derive the limit distribution of the statistics under the null hypothesis and under contiguous alternatives: a weighted chi-square distribution with $L-s$ terms, where $L$ is the number of inspection times and $s$ the number of parameters. The critical values are obtained by plugging the estimated weights into Imhof's formula, and the procedure has asymptotic size $\alpha$. A local-power analysis and a simulation study show that the cumulative statistics are more powerful than Pearson's statistic against a wrong lifetime distribution, and that the limit distribution is accurate already with $50$ devices. An application to light bulbs tested under step voltage illustrates the method.
item.dc:creator: Nirian Martin

item.title: Bayesian Calibration of Computer Experiments and Extrapolation
item.description: arXiv:2611.29567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Calibration, a fundamental inverse problem in uncertainty quantification, suffers from model identifiability issues. While the discrepancy decomposition model partially addresses this via a first-order Taylor expansion, it struggles when the approximation is biased. We propose a Bayesian modified discrepancy decomposition model that incorporates a residual process to capture higher-order discrepancy structures. By jointly inferring calibration parameters and model discrepancies within a Bayesian framework, our model recovers more physically meaningful parameters and provides reliable uncertainty quantification. Crucially, this accurate parameter recovery enables reliable extrapolative prediction, a challenge current methods largely fail to address. We validate the approach through numerical studies and a real-world industrial application: predicting the thermal stability of multilayer mirrors in extreme ultraviolet lithography. In this application, our method accurately predicts high-temperature responses far beyond the training domain, significantly outperforming existing calibration methods.
item.dc:creator: Jingyi Li, Shifeng Xiong

item.title: Directed Hypergraphs: Tensor Representation, Embedding Modeling, and Community Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.29655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Directed hypergraphs, in which each hyperedge connects a set of tail nodes to a set of head nodes, are the natural representation for many-to-many interactions in citation networks, metabolic pathways, and group communications. Despite their broad applicability, community detection for directed hypergraphs remains statistically underdeveloped: most existing methods either collapse hyperedges into pairwise edges, treat the two sides as interchangeable, or require the number of communities to be known. We propose a statistical framework for simultaneous embedding and community detection in nonuniform directed hypergraphs. The method allows each node to have distinct roles as a source and as a target, accommodates varying hyperedge sizes, and automatically determines the unknown numbers of communities on both sides, which need not be equal, through a fusion-penalized likelihood. We establish consistency of the estimated numbers of communities, exact recovery of both membership structures, and consistent probability tensor estimation. We further show that exact recovery is attainable without knowing the numbers of communities by a procedure that does not rely on any particular local solution, and we complement the upper bounds with a minimax lower bound for probability tensor estimation and a necessary condition for exact recovery. To ground the methodology, we construct the Cross-Statistics Citation Network, a new large-scale corpus linking Statistics with Biology, Computer Science, and Economics. Applying our method to this corpus reveals source and target roles of author communities in cross-field knowledge flow, and a pairwise representation of the same citations partly merges these roles.
item.dc:creator: Guojun Zhu, Haofei Wang, Mingyang Ren

item.title: Model-Averaged Shrinkage Estimation of the Spectral Density Using Welch's Method
item.description: arXiv:2611.29781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a shrinkage estimator of the spectral density based on a three-level hierarchical model. At the first level, we smooth Welch's spectral density estimator and model it as arriving from a Gaussian distribution centered at the true spectral density. In the second level, we place a normal prior on the true spectral density. We center this prior at a spectral density estimated assuming the data from an ARMA($p$,$q$) process. From these two levels, we create a conditionally specified shrinkage estimator. The conditional specification, of course, is the order of the ARMA process, i.e., the values of $p$ and $q$. We avoid selecting a particular order by creating a third level in which priors are placed on $p$ and $q$. Our final estimator is then a weighted average of shrinkage estimators. The average is taken over a set of ARMA($p$, $q$) models, and the weights are governed by the posteriors of $p$ and $q$. The methods introduced in this paper are similar to those presented in Botts and Daniels, but distinct from them in one critical way: the first level of the hierarchy. In the first level of our model, we borrow from recently developed theoretical results of Welch's spectral density estimator. Our estimator is consistent, computationally simple, and has performance comparable (and often superior) to other estimators.
item.dc:creator: Carsten Botts

item.title: The Coupled Scaled Dirichlet Distribution
item.description: arXiv:2611.29840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a coupled scaled Dirichlet distribution for paired compositions that may have different dimensions. Building on the matched Gamma-sharing construction of Trick, Rothkopf, and J\"akel (2023) for ordinary Dirichlet vectors, we allow scaled Dirichlet margins and extend the construction to include crossed sharing between non-corresponding latent components. We propose a signed coupling parameter whose sign selects matched or crossed sharing and whose magnitude controls the strength of sharing. We then develop a time-varying extension in which observed covariates determine this parameter. The model can therefore switch between matched and crossed sharing over time while preserving both scaled Dirichlet margins. We derive the joint mixed moments and use them to estimate dependence after fitting the margins separately. The moments can be evaluated by Monte Carlo simulation or by two-dimensional numerical quadrature, regardless of the dimensions of the compositions. Simulations show that the estimator generally recovers the sharing pattern, although weak crossed sharing is harder to detect. In an application to four U.S. equity-index futures, the time-varying model modestly improved the held-out energy and variogram scores for the trading-volume and intraday price-range compositions relative to the static-dependence model.
item.dc:creator: Jared N. Lakhani

item.title: Identification multiplicity across study designs
item.description: arXiv:2611.29908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The answer to a causal question often admits several translations in terms of observed data. These may differ in adjustment sets, comparison groups, instruments, mediators, cutoffs, eligibility occasions, or data sources. We describe the resulting collection of analyses by three structures: the causal target that each analysis identifies under its assumptions, the assumptions that the analyses share, and the sampling dependence among their estimates. A single decomposition separates identification discrepancies from differences in causal targets, and we make both terms explicit in fourteen examples spanning adjustment, comparative panels, proxies, mediators, instruments, discontinuities, staggered adoption, sequential trials, and source combination. Comparisons within a collection can reveal differential violations of assumptions but not a bias common to all analyses; agreement is therefore evidence about the assumptions that differ, not about those that are shared. Averaging retains a causal interpretation in three ways: efficient combination of analyses that identify one target, a projection of a causal curve with a declared approximating family and weighting measure, and inference under weaker premises such as validity of at least one analysis or a known sign of its bias. Precision weights, regression-implied weights, and hierarchical models do not supply these interpretations by themselves. We relate this account to triangulation, overidentification, marginal treatment effects, transportability, and recent methods for inference under model uncertainty, and distinguish identification multiplicity from multiple testing.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Garc\'ia Meixide, David R\'ios Insua

item.title: A Tensor Neural Network for Interpretable and Predictive Representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.29917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tensor regression is challenged by the exponential dimensionality of tensor-valued covariates and their complex multi-mode dependence. Existing methods therefore often rely on simple models, such as linear tensor regression and tensor additive models, which are computationally tractable but impose restrictive structural assumptions and may limit predictive accuracy. To address these limitations, we propose a tensor neural network that learns low-dimensional, interpretable, and prediction-sufficient representations while preserving the multi-mode structure of tensor data. The model captures nonlinear effects for accurate response prediction while retaining the interpretability of classical linear tensor regression. Theoretically, we establish selection consistency for the minimal representation dimension $K^*$ necessary for prediction and show that the estimator attains a representation-adaptive non-asymptotic error rate. Specifically, the rate improves from the ambient-dimensional order $n^{-\frac{\beta}{\mathcal{D}+2\beta}}$ to $n^{-\frac{\beta}{K^*+2\beta}}$, where $\mathcal{D}=\prod_{j=1}^M P_j$ is the ambient dimension. This demonstrates that recovering the low-dimensional representation is crucial for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in tensor regression. Moreover, minimizing the derived generalization error bound yields explicit tuning-parameter choices for computationally lightweight tuning. Extensive simulations and real-data analyses show consistent performance across settings of varying complexity. Unlike black-box deep learning models, the framework supports direct visualization and interpretation of learned tensor representations without external post hoc tools.
item.dc:creator: Shuoli Chen, Zhiyao Tan, Li Liu, Huazhen Lin

item.title: Space-Time Covariance with Screening Effects, Markov Property, and Long-Range Dependence
item.description: arXiv:2611.29973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Constructing space-time covariance models is an essential task to account for spatio-temporal dependence. However, there is a lack of practical guidance for constructing new covariance constructions. This paper focuses on studying the interplay among three statistical properties: screening effect, Markov property, and long-range dependence for constructing desirable parsimonious space-time covariance functions. While these properties imply seemingly conflicting statistical practice, it is shown in this paper that closed-form parsimonious covariance functions that simultaneously possess all these properties could be constructed and may be desirable for understanding space-time dependence. To examine these properties, this paper first shows that the confluent hypergeometric (CH) covariance function has asymptotic screening effect even in long-range dependent regime. Then this paper provides theoretical characterizations on Markov property for the hierarchical mixture construction including a necessary and sufficient condition. To account for more practical structures, this paper constructs a flexible Lagrangian CH model with the time-lag varying smoothness and tail decay parameters via a hierarchical mixture approach. These properties are illustrated via simulation studies. The practical performance under these models is evaluated for the Irish wind data and the sea surface temperature data.
item.dc:creator: Zih-Bing Chen, Pulong Ma

item.title: Discovery-Targeted False Discovery Rate Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.30031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In exploratory multiple testing, the false discovery rate (FDR) is a commonly used error criterion, and existing methods typically take an FDR level and return a set of discoveries. However, scientists often begin with a target number of discoveries, and accept any FDR level below a reasonable upper limit. Motivated by this practical need, we develop an FDR control approach with a data-driven, discovery-targeted level, which uses synthetic null p-values to split the p-value information between level selection and multiple testing. For independent p-values, the proposal controls finite-sample FDR given the reported level, which can therefore be interpreted in the standard way of a prespecified level. Asymptotically, the number of discoveries and the reported FDR level converge to the target and the optimal value. We also extend the approach to conformal p-values and to include a null proportion estimate. In simulations and real-data examples, the procedure yields a number of discoveries close to the target and smaller FDR levels compared with methods based on e-values or simultaneous false discovery proportion bounds.
item.dc:creator: Zijun Gao

item.title: Empirical Null Estimation via Adaptive Shifting and Tail Reconstruction for Large-Scale Multiple Testing
item.description: arXiv:2611.30122v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dependence among test statistics can produce complex empirical null shapes that are poorly captured by conventional parametric models. We propose TRAIL (Tail Reconstruction via Adaptive Iterative Learning), a method that estimates the pooled conditional null under a Gaussian factor model using a Gaussian-Hermite expansion without requiring the null correlation matrix as input. The procedure progressively reconstructs the potentially contaminated tail by generating pseudo-observations and retaining them in successive blocks from the initial cutoff outward. Its implementation, TRAIL_BIC, jointly selects the Gaussian reference location and Hermite truncation order using a BIC-type criterion. We characterize its limiting behavior and establish pooled-null consistency, together with asymptotic false discovery rate control and recovery of pooled oracle power under suitable conditions. Simulations across diverse dependence structures and null shapes show generally more stable false discovery behavior than competing empirical null methods with competitive power. An application to 48 coronary artery disease studies illustrates the method's flexibility in capturing complicated empirical shapes and its ability to identify more discoveries on average than the competing empirical null procedures.
item.dc:creator: Kyuram Kim, Junsik Kim, Junyong Park

item.title: Assumptions, Modeling and Risks: Applying ICH M15 to Statistical Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.30411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many instances in phase II and III clinical trials, critical assumptions underlying statistical analyses require discussion with regulators and other stakeholders. Such discussions benefit from a guiding process to promote consistency and clarity, but no widely and consistently applied framework currently exists. In January 2026, the International Council for Harmonisation released the ICH M15 Guideline on General Principles for Model-Informed Drug Development, which proposes a systematic framework for evaluating mechanistic models to support regulatory and development decisions. Although it focuses on mechanistic modeling, its structured assessment of model risks and benefits may be equally applicable to other approaches typically requiring a thorough appraisal of methodology and alignment among stakeholders, such as external data use and parametric longitudinal data analysis, and novel methodological approaches more generally. We illustrate and discuss how systematic risk-benefit evaluation of statistical models under the ICH M15 framework could work and propose its use to support acceptance of context-specific modeling strategies and to enhance decision-making transparency.
item.dc:creator: Tobia Mielke, Mouna Akacha, Christian Stock, Marc Vandemeulebroecke, Cornelia Ursula Kunz, Fei Chen, Simon Newsome

item.title: Spectral Regularization Beyond Ridge Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.30440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Inclusive Ridge (IR), a two-parameter spectral regularization family that contains ridge regression as well as iterated Tikhonov regularization. We derive its exact finite-sample coefficient risk and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for increasing or decreasing the additional filter-shape parameter around the ridge baseline to locally lower risk. We show that oracle-tuned ridge is generically suboptimal within the IR family. Under joint divergence of the penalty and filter order, we show that a nondegenerate spectral limit exists precisely when their ratio converges to a positive finite constant, yielding a continuous exponential filter. Along the fixed effective-scale path, we also obtain an exact risk-difference comparison and explicit sufficient conditions under which both higher-order estimators and the exponential limiting filter strictly outperform oracle-tuned ridge. In this regime, IR becomes progressively less sensitive to perturbations in the absolute penalty parameter while retaining sensitivity to its effective spectral scale, and a plug-in coefficient-risk first-order condition coincides with a degrees-of-freedom-adjusted discrepancy equation. Numerical examples based on the Fredholm inverse problem, tomographic reconstruction, a regression design, and synthetic difference-in-differences donor-weight estimation illustrate both the potential gains and the limitations of feasible tuning, distinguishing oracle improvements from gains attainable with estimated tuning parameters.
item.dc:creator: Kathryn Vasilaky, Walter Vasilaky

item.title: Robust Mixture Regressions and EM Algorithms via the Log-Truncated Likelihood
item.description: arXiv:2611.30635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite mixture regression is sensitive to gross residual outliers when component errors are modeled by Gaussian likelihoods. We propose a log-truncated likelihood for mixture regression. The likelihood is obtained by integrating a logarithmically growing Catoni-type score and exponentiating the negative integrated score, producing a proper location-scale density with a reusable normalizing constant and EM-compatible responsibilities. Although the induced density itself is lighter than exponential and has all moments, its likelihood score grows only logarithmically; this distinction yields a smooth residual-robust estimator that can be stably fitted when the data are generated from Laplace, Pareto, or even infinite-variance heavy-tailed error mechanisms. We derive deterministic tail envelopes, the location-scale decomposition of the normalizing constant, a rejection sampler, a lower-bounded mixing-weight update, a unique componentwise scale update, and a constrained generalized EM algorithm. The theory gives monotonicity of the observed likelihood and a local population-to-sample perturbation guarantee under standard compactness, contraction, and numerical-accuracy conditions. Simulations and applications to insurance claim severity and crypto return innovations show that the method is a competitive smooth likelihood-based alternative to Gaussian and pseudo-robust EM procedures, especially in residual-outlier regimes, while also clarifying its limitations under high leverage and extremely adversarial contamination.
item.dc:creator: Huiming Zhang, Longkun Hao

item.title: Bayesian sequential decision-making for adaptive early warning of bridge failure risk
item.description: arXiv:2611.30706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As a critical functionality of structural health monitoring (SHM) systems, early warning of increased bridge failure risk is essential for structural safety. However, traditional methods treat early warning merely as passive detection against a fixed safety limit and neglect evolving uncertainties and the economic consequences of decisions, leading to delayed alarms that increase the failure risk and hinder reliable and rational decision-making. This study formulates the early warning of increased structural failure risk as a sequential decision-making problem and develops a Bayesian framework for its solution. The presented framework unifies a probabilistic state transition model, an observation prediction model, cost models for early warning decisions, and a threshold-based decision strategy into a closed loop encompassing update, prediction, optimization, and decision execution. The structural state is updated iteratively via Bayes' theorem upon the arrival of new monitoring data, ensuring each decision is conditioned on the latest information. Through pre-posterior analysis over predicted future observations, the warning threshold is optimized by minimizing the expected total cost, which explicitly balances structural failure risks against warning response costs. In this way, the warning paradigm is shifted from passive detection to proactive decision-making, with the warning threshold adaptively updated as uncertainties and costs evolve. The framework was verified via two bridge case studies covering typical scenarios that lead to increased structural failure risk, including steel truss member fracture and stay cable rupture. Results demonstrate that warning decisions can be triggered in a timely and effective manner before severe consequences occur.
item.dc:creator: Teng Li, James L. Beck, Yong Huang, Hui Li, Hongju Han

item.title: Identification of Poisson processes through a one-dimensional projection
item.description: arXiv:2611.30756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the identification of stationary Poisson processes in Euclidean space through a single one-dimensional projection. Given a point process and a straight line, each point is retained independently with a probability given by a Gaussian function of its distance to the line; the retained points are projected onto the line. If the process is Poisson, the projection is again Poisson. What a single projection reveals depends on the sign of the second factorial cumulant, which is also the sign of the two-point correlations. Under a Palm domination condition, which holds for positively associated processes, the cumulant is nonnegative. Using a Chen-Stein argument we show that when the cumulant of the projection vanishes, the process is Poisson. Consequently, a single projection identifies non-Poissonianity. The same result holds under negative association. When the cumulant changes sign, a random projection detects a nonzero cumulant with probability one. We propose a test whose rejection region is computed by Monte Carlo. The test, together with a spacings-based variant for repulsive alternatives, rejects determinantal, shot-noise and other classical processes. When applied to lunar impact craters, the test rejects the Poisson hypothesis for craters with diameter below 30 km and does not reject it for craters above 45 km.
item.dc:creator: Pablo A. Ferrari, Ricardo Fraiman, Sebastian Grynberg, Leonardo Moreno

item.title: Interpretable Discovery of Heterogeneous Causal Dose-Response Curves
item.description: arXiv:2611.30838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discovering subgroups with heterogeneous treatment effects is a central task in causal inference. While methods for heterogeneous effect discovery have proliferated for discrete treatments, their counterparts for continuous treatments remain underdeveloped. In this paper, we introduce a novel, data-adaptive algorithm for discovering interpretable subgroups with heterogeneous causal dose-response curves. This algorithm combines doubly-robust dose-response curve estimation with recursive partitioning, using flexible objective functions to quantify heterogeneity across potential subgroups' dose-response curves. First, we show that the standard doubly-robust pseudo-outcome for continuous treatments cannot serve this purpose. We therefore construct the pseudo-outcome separately for each candidate subgroup, using subgroup-specific g-computation and a subgroup-specific stabilizing density. Finally, we characterize the differences between dose-response curves detected by each objective function. We establish uniform convergence of the splitting criteria and give conditions for recovery of the population greedy tree. We apply it to county-level data on fine particulate matter pollution (PM2.5) and mortality in the contiguous United States over the period 2000-2019. The discovered heterogeneous subgroups vary by education, income, and race. The proposed algorithm is implemented in the R package discoverHTE.
item.dc:creator: Falco J. Bargagli-Stoffi, Duy Pham, Edward H. Kennedy, Heejun Shin, Noah Greifer, Kevin P. Josey, Rachel C. Nethery

item.title: Quantifying and calibrating precision gain from covariate adjustment in clinical trials with binary endpoints
item.description: arXiv:2611.30845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Covariate adjustment is widely used in randomized clinical trials to improve estimation and inference of treatment effects. For continuous endpoints, the reasoning is straightforward: prognostic baseline covariates explain outcome variability and thereby increase precision. For binary endpoints, however, the situation is more complex because conditional and marginal effects generally differ in nonlinear outcome models such as logistic regression. We develop a theoretical framework for quantifying the maximum attainable first-order precision gain from covariate adjustment when estimating marginal treatment effects for binary endpoints. We derive a closed-form identity showing that precision-gain potential is governed by an estimand- and allocation-specific combination of the treatment-specific risk functions. Building on this identity, we introduce marginal prognostic strength as a population-level measure of prognostic information and characterize when it determines precision-gain potential and when the two quantities decouple. Specifically, substantial prognostic information within both treatment arms need not translate into improved precision for the marginal treatment effect when covariates are predictive on the target effect scale. We further develop a calibration algorithm for methodological simulation studies that preserves prespecified conditional outcome structures and marginal risks while allowing data-generating mechanisms to be calibrated by marginal prognostic strength and evaluated in terms of estimand-specific precision-gain potential. Together, these results provide a theoretical and practical framework for understanding, quantifying, and calibrating potential precision gains from covariate adjustment for binary endpoints.
item.dc:creator: Jannik Hammerschmied, Christian Stock, Martin Schnuerch

item.title: $K$-Midranks: A robust clustering algorithm for heavy-tailed data with applications to spectroscopy and finance
item.description: arXiv:2611.30953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clustering data with extreme observations and heavy tails can be challenging for methods that rely on distances between raw observations or specific distributional assumptions. We introduce $K$-midranks, a clustering method that replaces observations with coordinatewise ranks and partitions the transformed data using a procedure analogous to $K$-means. This transformation reduces the influence of extreme values while preserving the ordering of observations within each variable. We evaluate $K$-midranks against $K$-means, $K$-medoids, and mixture models based on Gaussian, Student's t, Cauchy, and generalized hyperbolic distributions through simulation studies, and provide some theoretical properties. $K$-midranks generally outperforms the competing methods on Cauchy-shifted data. In contrast, $K$-means and model-based methods perform better on Gaussian data and Student's t data with three degrees of freedom. We demonstrate the method's practical use in grouping samples based on Raman and LIBS spectra and clustering S\&P 500 stocks according to their returns. $K$-midranks achieves competitive performance with model-based methods in the spectroscopy applications and the best performance among the methods considered in the stock-return application. These findings suggest that $K$-midranks provides a useful alternative for clustering data with Cauchy-like heavy tails. An R package implementing the proposed method is available.
item.dc:creator: Larry Goldstein, Nathakhun Wiroonsri

item.title: CASPER: Discovering Spatially Resolved Causal Cell-Cell Communications
item.description: arXiv:2611.31108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics can reveal where ligands and receptors are expressed together. A harder question is whether exposure to a ligand changes pathway activity in nearby cells, since the same tissue environment can influence both ligand expression and pathway activity. We introduce CASPER, a Bayesian structural equation model that adjusts for receptor expression and represents the shared tissue environment with a Gaussian Markov random field. We show that the ligand-exposure effect is identifiable when the spatial covariance is known and distinguishable from independent noise, the coefficients are constant, and the structural errors are independent and homoskedastic. In simulations, CASPER reduced the bias seen in ordinary regression and in a regression that accounted for spatial dependence only in the outcome. We compared CASPER with CellPhoneDB in four public Xenium datasets. In ovarian cancer, CellPhoneDB found evidence of ligand--receptor expression enrichment for both IL6 and VEGFA. CASPER found greater support for a positive effect of fibroblast IL6 on the inflammatory-response score of ciliated epithelial cells than for an effect of fibroblast VEGFA on the angiogenesis score of endothelial cells. Code accompanies the Supplementary Materials and is available at https://github.com/nySTAT/casperCCC.
item.dc:creator: Yang Ni

item.title: Score-aware nonparametric adaptation of prediction-powered inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.31138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prediction-powered inference supplements labelled data with unlabelled data and external predictions to improve statistical efficiency. For inference on generalized linear model (GLM) coefficients, optimal use of these predictions generally requires estimating a conditional mean given the covariates and the external prediction, which can be challenging when the labelled data are limited or the covariates are multi-dimensional. We address this challenge through dimension reduction. We first fit an augmented generalized linear model combining the covariates and external prediction to obtain a scalar index, and then approximate the conditional mean by a univariate function of this index. Based on this construction, we develop a class of estimators for GLM coefficients and select the proposed estimator by minimizing the estimated asymptotic covariance trace. Under regularity conditions, the proposed estimator is asymptotically normal and has an asymptotic covariance trace no greater than that of the labelled-only estimator, even when the dimension reduction is insufficient. We also establish conditions under which the dimension reduction is sufficient. Simulations show that the proposed estimator is generally close to the best feasible estimator in root mean squared error, with confidence interval coverage close to the nominal level.
item.dc:creator: Xin Lu, Xuming He, Bo Li

item.title: From Multi-site Kaplan-Meier Curves to Evidence Synthesis: An Empirical Evaluation of IPD Reconstruction and Reconstruction-Assisted Meta-Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.31157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective. To compare methods for reconstructing individual participant data (IPD) from Kaplan-Meier (KM) curves and evaluate their use when reported trial estimates are unavailable for meta-analysis. Materials and Methods. We compared iterative inverse-KM (iKM), IPDfromKM, KMtoIPD, and quadratic programming (QP) using their specified packages and auxiliary inputs. The single-trial benchmark evaluated curve agreement, event and risk-set accuracy, and treatment-effect accuracy across different survival settings. The meta-analysis benchmark compared omission of trials with unavailable estimates against four hybrid strategies that retained reported estimates and reconstructed missing estimates under missing-completely-at-random reporting. Results. Relative method performance varied by setting and accuracy measure. Accurate reproduction of curves or supplied risk tables did not consistently identify the smallest treatment-effect errors. In 30-trial meta-analyses with 80% of reported hazard ratios unavailable, hybrids retained 27.9-30.0 trials, compared with 6.0 for omission, and achieved pooled log-hazard-ratio root-mean-squared error of 0.0356-0.0371 versus 0.0852. Discussion. The comparisons reflect method-specific inputs, including accurately supplied auxiliary information, rather than algorithms receiving identical information. Controlled coordinate perturbation did not reproduce full image-digitization error. Conclusion. Reconstruction should be selected and evaluated for its intended analytical use. Under the tested conditions, hybrid strategies supported meta-analysis by supplementing unavailable compatible trial estimates.
item.dc:creator: Hui Yao, Nazmul Islam, Yicheng Shen, Lang Lang, Yanxun Xu, Jiayi Tong

item.title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.28342v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.
item.dc:creator: Xin Xu

item.title: Geometric ergodicity of Gibbs samplers for linear mixed models with several heavy-tailed random-effect components and unknown tail parameters
item.description: arXiv:2611.28413v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Linear mixed models with heavy-tailed random effects are widely used for robust Bayesian analysis of longitudinal data. We study the three-block Gibbs sampler for such models when the random effects are split into several components, such as random intercepts and slopes, each with its own scale and its own scale mixture of normals, when the tail parameters have priors on finite grids and are drawn jointly with the latent weights, and when the random-effects design is rank deficient, as when some subjects contribute a single observation. We give sufficient conditions for geometric ergodicity that attribute the rank deficiency to the components that cause it, and show that, under conditions on the gamma priors on the precision parameters, they hold for Student-t and slash random effects with individual weights, any grid of tail parameters and any design. The result extends to random-effect vectors whose coordinates share a weight, for subject-specific designs with known shape matrices. It justifies Monte Carlo standard errors for regression coefficients, log-scales and posterior probabilities of the tail parameters. Simulations show that the scale and the tail parameter can mix much more slowly than the regression coefficients, and an analysis of beta-HCG data illustrates the methods.
item.dc:creator: Rolando de la Cruz, Nathalie Humeniy

item.title: Neural-network-powered new-physics searches by predictive goodness of fit
item.description: arXiv:2611.28414v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Model-independent searches for new physics test whether data agree with a Reference model with unknown nuisance parameters. Because the shape and location of a signal are not specified, these tests call for flexible learners (fitting procedures such as neural networks), and a likelihood ratio maximized over a neural network falls outside the standard asymptotic theory, making the calibration a major challenge. We propose a predictive alternative: the departure from the Reference is fitted on part of the data and its likelihood gain over the fitted Reference is evaluated on the rest, cross-fitted over several folds to preserve sample efficiency. The nuisance estimation error is propagated into the variance of the test statistic to first order, in the spirit of Neyman's C(alpha) test, so that the test need not be recalibrated at each nuisance value. The randomness in the fitted departure is treated by a central limit theorem for cross-validated statistics under algorithmic stability, plus a variance correction when stability is not achieved. The calibration is analytic, and no pseudo-experiments are needed. On established one-dimensional and five-dimensional (dilepton) benchmarks, the false-positive rate always stays within Monte Carlo error of nominal across different nuisances and the learners' tuning. The test's power relative to existing learned tests is mixed: higher for some signals and lower for others, depending on how well the fitted departure captures the signal.
item.dc:creator: Jing Lei

item.title: Targeted Learning for Externally Controlled Trials and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2611.28421v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper focuses on externally controlled trials (ECTs), which consist of a single-arm clinical trial supplemented by an external control arm (ECA). Potential data sources for the ECA can be broadly classified into three categories: (i) the control arm of a historical clinical trial, (ii) a concurrent cohort study, and (iii) external real-world data (RWD). In this paper, we consider a broad class of estimands defined through balancing weights. For a given estimand in the class, we discuss the efficient influence function (EIF) and the targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE), together with practical implementation algorithms. Within the targeted learning framework, TMLE is a substitution estimator that enjoys several desirable theoretical properties and favorable finite-sample performance. Finally, the proposed framework is extended to two additional settings: (1) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) augmented with external covariate information to define a target population, and (2) indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) that combine individual patient data (IPD) from an internal RCT with aggregate data (AgD) from an external RCT.
item.dc:creator: Yixin Fang, Weili He

item.title: KernelMix: Bayesian kernel machine regression in Python
item.description: arXiv:2611.28634v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exposures measured together can have nonlinear associations with an outcome, and the association with one exposure may depend on another. Bayesian kernel machine regression represents these patterns through a flexible exposure-response function. We implement this approach in KernelMix, a Python package. To handle different outcome types, KernelMix combines the exposure function with continuous, binary, count and survival models, including selected extensions for clustered observations and censored event times. For fitted models, it returns posterior summaries, uncertainty intervals, joint predictions and sampling diagnostics. Fitting and prediction use NumPy and SciPy without requiring R. To assess the implementation, we compare selected Gaussian and probit posterior summaries and conditional calculations with installed R bkmr 0.2.2 and check additional model components against independent mathematical calculations. A daily ozone analysis illustrates how these components form an analysis workflow.
item.dc:creator: Nilson Chapagain

item.title: Tuning the false discovery rate in the closed eBH procedure
item.description: arXiv:2611.28708v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The closed eBH procedure controls the false discovery rate under arbitrary dependence between the input e-values. It takes the target false discovery rate $\alpha$ as its input and outputs a rejection set $R$, the usual goal being to maximize its size $\left|R\right|$. This note discusses a modification of the closed eBH procedure that allows choosing the target false discovery rate post hoc: the rejection set and its level $\alpha$ can be chosen after seeing the data, and the expected ratio of the false discovery proportion to $\alpha$ is at most 1. We adapt Vovk and Wang's (2023) algorithm for computing discovery e-matrices to computing, in quadratic time, the frontier of achievable combinations $(\left|R\right|,\alpha)$ of the size of a rejection set $R$ and its level $\alpha$. The frontier allows us to compute an optimal rejection set in view of a given utility function $F$, $F(\left|R\right|,\alpha)\to\max$, striking a balance between the goals of reducing $\alpha$ and increasing $\left|R\right|$.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Vovk

item.title: Robust Pair--Restricted Lipschitz Regression with Global--Local Transfer
item.description: arXiv:2611.28936v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a robust pair-restricted Lipschitz regression framework for grouped longitudinal data represented as finite trajectories in a space equipped with a prescribed or learned pseudometric. For a fixed geometry, latent responses and a Lipschitz bound are estimated jointly through a convex optimisation problem with constraints imposed on selected trajectory pairs. We show that the choice of fidelity loss leads to different structural behaviour: Huber regularisation strictly reduces the pair-restricted Lipschitz seminorm whenever the exact interpolant has a finite positive seminorm, whereas $L^1$ fidelity can preserve exact interpolation below a data-dependent threshold. For grouped observations, global and local Lipschitz structures are combined while keeping group identity outside the trajectory geometry. The global component draws on observations from other groups, while the local component uses each group's history to account for group-specific behaviour. We also characterise when group-specific observations can be fitted exactly under a shared Lipschitz bound and establish a regularity bound for the combined predictor. We describe a computational implementation based on constraint generation and illustrate the framework through an application to longitudinal sow-production data.
item.dc:creator: Sergi Sanjuan, Enrique A. S\'anchez P\'erez, Roger Arnau

item.title: Stochastic non-metric MDS for noisy high-dimensional data
item.description: arXiv:2611.28985v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) constructs low-dimensional embeddings that approximate pairwise distances in a high-dimensional dataset. MDS exists in several flavors, with metric MDS approximating distances directly and non-metric MDS additionally optimizing for an arbitrary monotonic transformation of the high-dimensional distances. Empirically, metric MDS is known to suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Here we extend prior theoretical results for metric MDS on fully uninformative data to a more general case of finite, high-dimensional data with concentrated distances. We show that the metric MDS embeddings of such datasets stay distributionally close to the data-independent limit case. We then show that non-metric MDS is more robust to high-dimensional noise and can yield informative embeddings of such data. While existing implementations of non-metric MDS are slow, we develop a fast implementation using stochastic gradient descent in PyTorch. Using our implementation, we conduct an empirical study using multiple simulated and real-world datasets, including population-genomic and scRNA-seq data, and show that non-metric MDS can strongly outperform other methods in terms of global structure preservation.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Damrich, Dmitry Kobak

item.title: Zero-Shot Prognostic Covariate Adjustment and Mechanistic Week-1 Myelosuppression Updating Across 9,500 Oncology Patients Under FDA Guidance
