item.description: arXiv:2611.28991v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The FDA's 2023 guidance on covariate adjustment recommends "that sponsors adjust for covariates that are anticipated to be most strongly associated with the outcome of interest" and notes that "it may be useful to use previous studies (e.g. a Phase 2 trial) to select prognostic covariates or form prognostic indices." Its August 2024 guidance on dosage optimization, part of Project Optimus, states that "the dose- and exposure-response relationships should be evaluated to select a dosage(s) for clinical trial(s)." We analyzed the control arms of 14 randomized trials from Project Data Sphere, with 5,074 patients with overall survival follow-up, in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), and in three AACR Project GENIE Biopharma Collaborative cohorts (4,440 patients). In all, about 9,500 patients were studied. We used the regularized baseline prognostic index to compute out-of-fold estimates of the share of covariate-adjusted log-rank variance removed ($\rho^2$), and found these to be 0.177 to 0.186 for the three indications. For the locked held-out trials, the value was 0.183 (second-line NSCLC docetaxel), 0.177 (first-line PDAC gemcitabine) and 0.110 (first-line mCRC FOLFOX plus bevacizumab). Refitting in GENIE BPC resulted in estimates of 0.073 to 0.127 for first-line and 0.122 to 0.219 for later lines. In a simulated 600-patient trial, 5,000 within-stratum re-randomizations gave a type I error rate of 0.051 for the adjusted test. At $\rho^2 = 0.18$, adjustment raises power from 80.0% to 87.2%, cuts required events by 18% or shrinks the control arm by about 30%. A Friberg marrow prior updated with week 1 blood counts raised the AUROC for new cycle 1 grade 3 or worse neutropenia from 0.791 to 0.816 (n = 3,465; calibration slope 0.999; Brier skill 0.190) and raised it in 5 of 8 cross-trial rows (up to +0.116).
item.dc:creator: Varshal Patel, Neema Darabi

item.title: Community Detection in Fuzzy Social Networks through Fuzzy Co-Membership Relations over Alpha-Cut Realizations
item.description: arXiv:2611.29342v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In fuzzy social networks the ties between actors are triangular fuzzy numbers, and community detection applied to their cores ignores how the partition depends on their vagueness. We propose a fuzzy co-membership relation obtained by running the Louvain algorithm on crisp networks compatible with the alpha-cuts of the ties and integrating the proportions of co-assignment over alpha. The relation is positive semidefinite; from it we derive a consensus partition, the number of groups, membership degrees and an assignment ambiguity index. In simulations from stochastic block models the relation does not yield better partitions than symmetric perturbations of the cores of the same size. Its ambiguity index is more closely associated with the structural position of the actors and identifies actors split between two groups when the vagueness is concentrated on them; when the asymmetry of the fuzzy ties points towards the latent tie strength, its co-membership degrees have a lower Brier score. The interval-weighted Louvain algorithm estimates the number of communities more accurately. In two departmental collaboration networks the observed ambiguity is lower than under permuted ratings, while the partitions depend on the symmetrization of directed ratings and on the coding of non-response.
item.dc:creator: Annamaria Porreca, Fabrizio Maturo

item.title: Exact, narrow and fast: Use the Gaffke confidence interval for the mean of a discrete bounded variable
item.description: arXiv:2611.29512v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Survey ratings, test scores and many other data take a few known values, and we often want a confidence interval for their mean. For small samples, or for means close to the smallest or largest value, the usual intervals cover the true mean much less often than they claim. The interval of Gaffke generalizes the Clopper-Pearson interval to any finite set of values, and a recent proof of Gaffke's conjecture shows that its coverage is at least the nominal level for every sample size and every distribution. Its endpoints, however, are quantiles of a weighted sum of Dirichlet variables, with no closed form. This note makes three contributions. First, a fast and accurate algorithm for the endpoints: a Fourier inversion integral on a line through the saddle point gives tail probabilities with a small relative error, a Gauss-Legendre rule on geometric panels converges at the same rate wherever the singularities are, and a Newton iteration needs 2.6 evaluations per endpoint on average. The cost is $O(kN)$ operations for $k$ values and $N$ quadrature nodes, and $N$ does not grow with the sample size, so an interval takes less than a millisecond for any $n$. Second, an experimental comparison with the published intervals: for $n \le 30$, the Gaffke interval is the shortest of the intervals that keep the level, 17 to 20% shorter than the betting interval of Waudby-Smith and Ramdas and 19 to 37% shorter than Anderson's, while the shorter intervals (Wald, Student, profile likelihood, Bayesian) cover the mean less than 50% of the time for some distributions. Third, tested Python and R packages and a web page, with endpoints accurate to $10^{-12}$ of the range of the values. So the interval is exact, narrow and fast, and we recommend it.
item.dc:creator: Louis Abraham

item.title: Sharpe Ratio Inference after Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.29747v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The economic value of return signals is often assessed using the Sharpe ratios of portfolios based on those signals. In modern asset pricing, return signals often depend on many features, including state variables and firm-specific characteristics, and machine-learning methods are increasingly used to estimate them. But how much confidence can we place in the estimated Sharpe ratios? We find that signal-estimation error can remain consequential for inference even in large asset panels. Moreover, pooling observations across assets does not necessarily make this uncertainty negligible when predictors contain common features or exhibit substantial cross-sectional dependence. As a remedy, we develop a debiased Sharpe-ratio estimator that accounts for signal-estimation error and provides valid confidence intervals and tests against benchmarks. Our target is the population Sharpe ratio of a specified portfolio rule evaluated at the true conditional expected returns given the features. The framework covers market-timing, long-short, and other signal-based portfolios, allowing the number of assets to grow with and greatly exceed the time-series sample size. The method combines orthogonal portfolio moments with time-series cross-fitting and remains valid under suitable estimation-error bounds for machine-learning forecasts. Empirically, we revisit the setting of Gu et al. (2020) using machine-learning estimators of the return signals. The strongest long-short Sharpe-ratio gains relative to market benchmarks remain significant after debiasing, providing statistical evidence of the economic value of their feature set. Conventional and debiased Sharpe-ratio estimates are generally similar, while the associated confidence intervals and tests can differ substantially. These differences vary across signal estimators and portfolio rules and do not uniformly weaken the evidence of portfolio performance.
item.dc:creator: Sander Barendse, Ming Cheng

item.title: Sequential Selection against an Adaptive Opponent
item.description: arXiv:2611.30006v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Selecting a strategy by testing it against an opponent is common in game-playing AI, red-teaming of language models, and safety evaluations of AI agents. In many of these settings, the opponent adapts to what it observes, so a strategy that keeps winning in practice may already have stopped working by the time it is used. Motivated by these settings, we study a player who tries strategies in practice games against an adaptive opponent, decides when to stop, and then either selects one strategy for the next game or abstains. The goal is to select a strategy that meets a target win probability while rarely selecting one that has already fallen below it. For a single strategy, we propose the Sequential Private Accumulated-excess Rule (SPAR), which accumulates evidence through a capped likelihood ratio and selects the strategy once this evidence reaches a privately drawn uniform threshold. We show that the stopping time must involve such private randomness. The number of games SPAR needs is inversely proportional to the error tolerance, and this rate is optimal even when the opponent happens not to adapt. To select among multiple strategies, we introduce Screen-then-SPAR, which screens candidates in stages before applying SPAR. The procedure adapts to the best strategy's unknown initial margin above the target and achieves the minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. The performance of Screen-then-SPAR is demonstrated through simulations and two real-data studies, one using recorded coding-agent attacks from MonitoringBench and the other using rock-paper-scissors matches between human players and an adaptive bot.
item.dc:creator: Zhongyuan Lyu, Xiaocong Xu

item.title: Model-Assisted Probability of Detection Studies for Image-Based Human Inspection
item.description: arXiv:2611.30032v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Establishing a probability of detection (POD) curve is important for assessing the reliability of components in aging systems. Traditional POD studies rely on physical specimens containing representative flaws and human inspectors who record detection results, making such studies costly. This paper demonstrates how appropriately validated physics-based simulation can substantially reduce, and in suitable applications potentially replace, physical POD experiments. We use XRSIM, an X-ray radiographic simulator, to generate weld images containing cracks of varying size, morphology, and location. Flaw characteristics, locations, and the number of flaws per image were randomized, with images containing zero to three flaws. Each simulated flaw is treated as an observational unit contributing flaw-level hit-miss responses. To capture human inspection variability, the images were presented in random order to five inspectors, each of whom inspected the images twice. The resulting data were analyzed using a repeated-measures binary-regression model accounting for flaw-to-flaw, inspector-to-inspector, flaw/inspector-combination, and inspection-to-inspection variability. Bayesian inference was used to estimate the population-mean POD curve, inspector-specific POD curves, and associated statistical uncertainty. Results show that flaw-to-flaw variability dominates, with appreciable differences among inspectors. The study provides a framework for combining physics-based image simulation with controlled human inspection to estimate POD while reducing the experimental burden of physical specimen fabrication.
item.dc:creator: Qizheng Xia, William Q. Meeker, Joseph N. Gray, Qing Li

item.title: How long must an honest confidence interval be after causal discovery? Benign and malignant weak edges
item.description: arXiv:2611.30256v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: After causal discovery, a confidence interval for a total effect valid uniformly over the model class must pay for structural uncertainty. We measure this price by the worst-case ratio of expected length to that of the efficient interval knowing the graph, for linear Gaussian models with a known superset of the adjacencies and k-triangle faithfulness. The global price is of order sqrt(n) once one edge can be malignant, so we study it locally, near a generic distribution with one edge absent. Our main result classifies this weak edge by Meek closures. It is benign if deleting it leaves the effect identifiable in the resulting MPDAG and Markov equivalent explanations agree; the local price is then bounded, and otherwise, for small k, of order sqrt(n). At benign edges the price is of order R+K, with R a ratio of efficient lengths and K a cross-model constant. It equals one, so that honesty is free, exactly when K = 0, generically decided by a d-separation. For two Markov classes it is determined within a factor 3.40, and its upper bound is approached without knowing the base point or the weak edge. A further graphical condition gives the rate uniformly in a second edge's margin.
item.dc:creator: Ruiqi Zhao

item.title: Tensor Recovery with Heterogeneous Mode Structures
item.description: arXiv:2611.30435v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tensor recovery methods often impose a common structural assumption across modes, even when different modes may exhibit distinct forms of regularity. We propose a unified convex framework that treats each mode according to its structure. Smoothly varying modes form an indexing domain and are handled by local kernel weighting, whereas retained modes may receive low-rank, group-sparse, graph-Laplacian, or autoregressive regularization in distinct and potentially overlapping combinations. The framework also covers ordinary tensor recovery without local smoothing. A consensus HM-ADMM algorithm separates the active penalties into tractable proximal and linear-system updates. For the population-quadratic estimator, we derive deterministic oracle inequalities and high-probability bounds under independent trace regression. The bounds disentangle stochastic error, rank and support complexity, smoothing bias, and quadratic mismatch. They also identify when quadratic penalties sharpen the Frobenius-error bound. For regular smooth domains, the theory characterizes the bias-variance trade-off and yields an optimal bandwidth order, with a specialization to uniform tensor completion. Simulations and two applications illustrate the gains from matching regularization to mode-specific structure, especially under severe undersampling.
item.dc:creator: Zhixin Huang, Ziyuan Chen, Fang Yao, Ying Yang

item.title: Adaptive experiments with observational data: Efficient experimental design and asymptotic time-uniform inference for long-term treatment effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.30595v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Estimating long-term treatment effects in experiments requires waiting for outcomes to become observable, which can delay both the evaluation of an intervention and subsequent decisions. Recent econometric work has developed identification methods that combine experimental data with observational data containing long-term outcomes. This paper proposes using observational data available before the experiment begins not only for identification but also for designing adaptive experiments, in which experimental data are collected sequentially. To estimate the long-term average treatment effect as precisely as possible, we express its semiparametric efficiency bound as a function of the covariate sampling and treatment assignment rules and minimize the bound over these rules to characterize an optimal fixed experimental design. This experimental design depends on the treatment-specific conditional variances of the observational prediction of the long-term outcome, which can be learned only from experimental participants. We therefore construct a sequential procedure that learns the experimental design as experimental data accumulate and show that its estimator attains the same limiting variance as an oracle estimator implemented under the optimal fixed experimental design. We further construct an asymptotic confidence sequence whose coverage holds simultaneously over all rounds after a prespecified start, so that the experimenter can inspect the interval after each participant and stop once it excludes zero. Monte Carlo simulations show that the learned experimental design can improve precision and shorten the time to detection relative to baseline sampling and equal-probability assignment. An illustration using the Pakistan Graduation experiment shows how estimated conditional variance heterogeneity informs sampling and treatment assignment.
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Kawato

item.title: What Should an Experiment Measure? Combining a Short-Term Experiment with Confounded Observational Data to Identify Long-Term Treatment Effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.30599v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Observational data often record long-term outcomes but do not identify long-term treatment effects when selection depends on unrecorded characteristics, while randomized experiments remove this selection but require years of follow-up. We ask what a short-term experiment should measure so that, combined with observational data, it identifies the average long-term treatment effect in the observational population. In our main setting, the observational data record a coarse post-treatment measurement of the unrecorded characteristics but not a detailed measurement that would remove confounding. In this setting, we derive three implications for what the experiment should measure. It should (1) collect the same coarse measurement, (2) measure the characteristics in enough detail that conditioning on this detailed measurement and recorded covariates removes confounding and leaves the coarse measurement uninformative about selection and the treatment-specific long-term outcome mean, and (3) distinguish no more levels of the characteristics than the coarse measurement can separate. We characterize the treatment effect through linear inverse problems based on exclusion restrictions and completeness, and thereby show that combining such an experiment with the observational data identifies the effect. We propose an estimator that is based on the efficient influence function and removes the first-order effect of nuisance estimation errors. We give conditions under which this estimator is asymptotically normal and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. Cross-fitting relaxes the conditions on nuisance estimation. In simulations and a Job Corps illustration, the proposed Tikhonov-penalized series estimator has smaller absolute bias and coverage closer to the nominal level than competing estimators.
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Kawato

item.title: What Environment Invariance Identifies: Minimal Invariant Sets in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.30609v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Invariant causal prediction identifies the direct causes of a target $Y$ by searching for covariate sets whose conditional law of $Y$ is stable across environments. We state that criterion at the level of operators, calling a set $S$ invariant when the conditional mean embeddings of $Y$ given $X_S$ agree across environments, and characterise the resulting family exactly: under two conditions on the environments, which we state separately because they fail independently, the invariant sets are precisely those containing $PA(Y)$ and no descendant of $Y$. Two consequences follow. Invariance does not identify $PA(Y)$ uniquely, since every descendant-free superset is invariant as well; and $PA(Y)$ is the unique minimal invariant set. In finite samples, recovery requires the non-invariant sets to be separated from invariance by a margin, and the sample size splits into a screening term logarithmic in the ambient dimension and a term inherited from conditional mean embedding estimation, which is the binding one. The characterisation yields two selection rules with different failure modes, of which the conservative one controls false positives. Controlled experiments verify each population prediction directly, including the failure of uniqueness. They also show that invariance testing is a practical bottleneck: two natural designs are severely miscalibrated, while the selected test reduces but does not eliminate Type I error inflation.
item.dc:creator: Ridham Patel

item.title: Transport-Safe Evaluation of LLM Agents: Trajectory-Dependent Judge Error and Anytime-Valid Auditing
item.description: arXiv:2611.30742v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are often ranked by an LLM judge whose error rates are measured once and reused for every agent. The corrected success rates can then be biased when the judge's errors depend on the trajectory and agents differ in the trajectories they produce for successes or failures. We derive the exact asymptotic bias and give a chain of checks from identification to simultaneous ranks. On a four-agent semi-synthetic benchmark, a scalar correction with oracle calibration has maximum bias 0.245 and mean pointwise coverage 0.016, and never recovers the full ranking (0/250 replications). Augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) with a uniform or a design-aware random audit keeps the maximum bias below 0.003, with mean pointwise coverage of 0.939 and 0.950. In a 48-cell stress test, effective target support rises only from 0.209 to 0.805 as calibration grows from 600 to 4,800 labels, while audited AIPW keeps a mean absolute error of 0.018-0.020. Without calibration support, or with judge dependence within an externally justified bound, we report valid bounds or sensitivity sets and carry them into rank sets. An e-process confidence sequence stays valid, for a stable target, under predictable adaptive auditing and arbitrary stopping.

item.title: Fast and Consistent Structure Learning in Graphical Models via Approximate Cross-Validation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30822v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Structure learning for sparse graphical models in high dimensions requires both computational scalability and selection consistency. Classical criteria such as (Extended) Bayesian Information Criterion can provide consistency, but rely on model-specific likelihoods and complexity calibration. In comparison, cross-validation avoids such analytic calibration and is therefore attractive for graph learning. However, cross-validation is computationally infeasible and theoretically inconsistent in structure learning. This creates a tension between consistency and flexibility in modeling. In this work, we resolve the tension by developing a scalable graph-recovery procedure built on approximate cross-validation. We demonstrate its effectiveness in learning large graphical models both theoretically and empirically, and establish selection consistency under mild signal strength assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Lyu, Mladen Kolar, Bryon Aragam

item.title: Revealing Geometry under Strong Noise: Spectral Embeddings and Clustering via Random Geometric Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.31047v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern massive datasets often contain useful low-dimensional nonlinear structures that are hidden by noise. Spectral embedding algorithms rely on meaningful local relationships between observations, but noise accumulated across many coordinates can make the observed distances unreliable. This also complicates clustering when groups have curved or concentric shapes and cannot be distinguished by their centers. In this paper, we develop a new method that denoises pairwise distances before using them to construct spectral embeddings and identify communities. Our approach uses cross-fitted projections to estimate distances between the underlying signals, selects a neighborhood radius from the observed sample, and builds a random geometric graph whose spectral coordinates represent the latent geometric structure. By connecting nearby points, such a geometric graph can distinguish different groups even when their centers coincide. A novel recursive procedure is then proposed to extract clusters from the graph using its spectral embeddings when such clusters exist. On the theoretical side, under a manifold model, we provide guarantees for our spectral embedding algorithm, which can be understood through the eigendecomposition of an integral operator associated with the underlying geometry. We show that the algorithm is robust to noise when the total noise energy is comparable to the total signal energy or, under additional conditions, exceeds it. To our knowledge, this is among the first spectral embedding algorithms that can handle such strong noise in datasets with nonlinear structures. In addition, our proposed clustering algorithm can recover the underlying clusters even when their centers coincide. Numerical studies demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method in mitigating noise and revealing geometric structures for both spectral embedding and clustering.
item.dc:creator: Hai-Xiao Wang, Xiucai Ding

item.title: Decoupling Solving from Abstention: Single-Rollout Conformal Risk Control for Hard-Budget LLM Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2611.31065v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hard token budgets often interrupt LLM reasoning before an answer is produced. Forcing reasoning to terminate recovers correct solutions but also increases confident errors, creating a joint challenge of solving within budget and deciding when to abstain. Existing remedies are costly or lack guarantees: supervised fine-tuning offers no error control, penalizing wrong answers during reinforcement learning (RL) can suppress exploration, and multi-sample conformal methods multiply inference cost. We propose Tail-CRC, a single-rollout framework that separates candidate generation from submission control. We first adapt the solver to budget forcing with pure binary correctness rewards; after freezing it, we apply conformal risk control to upper-tail token surprise in the answer span. Each rollout yields both an answer and an uncertainty score from token log probabilities, enabling finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions under exchangeability and recalibration across risk targets or domains without retraining. We show that wrong-answer penalties create failure-only comparisons in group-relative RL, derive an exploration-starvation boundary, and identify length-induced ranking reversals and single-token spike sensitivity in answer scores. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B, 50 RL updates on 400 problems improve correct-submission rates by 15.0--29.6 points on DAPO and 4.3--12.8 points on out-of-domain Omni-MATH over inference-only budget forcing, while reducing generation cost by 3.5--12.6\%. On 8B Omni-MATH, target-domain calibration cuts wrong submissions from 30.3\% to 5.8\% at 4K and from 41.8\% to 6.5\% at 8K. At 4K, generation is 2.05$\times$ faster for 4B and 2.23$\times$ faster for 8B than unforced 8K decoding in local amortized batch time. Tail-CRC thus enables reliable, efficient budgeted reasoning from a single rollout.
item.dc:creator: Qianyi Chen, Bo Li

item.title: Robust Brain MRI Image Classification with SIBOW-SVM
item.description: arXiv:2311.08908v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Primary Central Nervous System tumors in the brain are among the most aggressive diseases affecting humans. Early detection and classification of brain tumor types, whether benign or malignant, glial or non-glial, is critical for cancer prevention and treatment, ultimately improving human life expectancy. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the most effective technique for brain tumor detection, generating comprehensive brain scans. However, human examination can be error-prone and inefficient due to the complexity, size, and location variability of brain tumors. Recently, automated classification techniques using machine learning methods, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have demonstrated significantly higher accuracy than manual screening. However, deep learning-based image classification methods, including CNNs, face challenges in estimating class probabilities without proper model calibration. In this paper, we propose a novel brain tumor image classification method called SIBOW-SVM, which integrates the Bag-of-Features model with SIFT feature extraction and weighted Support Vector Machines. This new approach can effectively extract hidden image features, enabling differentiation of various tumor types, provide accurate label predictions, and estimate probabilities of images belonging to each class, offering high-confidence classification decisions. We have also developed scalable and parallelable algorithms to facilitate the practical implementation of SIBOW-SVM for massive image datasets. To benchmark our method, we apply SIBOW-SVM to a public dataset of brain tumor MRI images containing four classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary, and normal. Our results demonstrate that the new method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, including CNNs, in terms of uncertainty quantification, classification accuracy, computational efficiency, and data robustness.
item.dc:creator: Liyun Zeng, Hao Helen Zhang

item.title: Probabilities for asymmetric p-outside values
item.description: arXiv:2410.15383v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In 2017-2020 Jordanova and co-authors investigate probabilities for p-outside values and determine them in many particular cases. They show that these probabilities are closely related to the concept for heavy tails. Tukey's boxplots are very popular and useful in practice. Analogously to the chi-square-criterion, the relative frequencies of the events an observation to fall in different their parts, compared with the corresponding probabilities an observation of a fixed probability distribution to fall in the same parts, help the practitioners to find the accurate probability distribution of the observed random variable. These open the door to work with the distribution sensitive estimators which in many cases are more accurate, especially for small sample investigations. All these methods, however, suffer from the disadvantage that they use inter quantile range in a symmetric way. The concept for outside values should take into account the form of the distribution. Therefore, here, we give possibility for more asymmetry in analysis of the tails of the distributions. We suggest new theoretical and empirical box-plots and characteristics of the tails of the distributions. These are theoretical asymmetric p-outside values functions. We partially investigate some of their properties and give some examples. It turns out that they do not depend on the center and the scaling factor of the distribution. Therefore, they are very appropriate for comparison of the tails of the distribution, and later on, for estimation of the parameters, which govern the tail behaviour of the cumulative distribution function.
item.dc:creator: Pavlina K. Jordanova

item.title: Causal tail coefficient for compound extremes in multivariate time series
item.description: arXiv:2509.19007v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Extreme events are often multivariate in nature. A compound extreme occurs when a combination of variables jointly produces a significant impact, even if individual components are not necessarily marginally extreme. Compound extremes have been observed across a wide range of domains, including space weather, climate, and environmental science. For example, a single episode of heavy rainfall can trigger a compound hydrological response involving elevated river levels, increased soil saturation, and substantial surface runoff, which together may result in a sustained flooding event. However, most existing methods for detecting extremal causality focus primarily on individual extreme values and lack the flexibility to capture causal relationships between compound extremes. This work introduces a novel framework for detecting causal dependencies between extreme events, including compound extremes. We introduce the compound causal tail coefficient for stationary time series, which quantifies the extremal dependence between an extreme in a candidate cause series and a subsequent compound response jointly defined by multiple future values of one or more effect series. Based on a consistent estimator of this coefficient, we develop a novel bootstrap hypothesis test to evaluate the presence and direction of causal relationships. Our method can accommodate nonlinearity and latent confounding variables. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by establishing theoretic properties, and through simulation studies and an application to space-weather data.
item.dc:creator: Cathy Yin, Adam M. Sykulski, Almut E. D. Veraart

item.title: Distribution-Free Prediction Sets for Regression under Target Shift
item.description: arXiv:2510.10985v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In real-world applications, the limited availability of labeled outcomes presents significant challenges for statistical inference due to high collection costs, technical barriers, and other constraints. In this work, we propose a method to construct efficient conformal prediction sets for new target outcomes by leveraging a source distribution that is distinct from the target but related through a distributional shift assumption and provides abundant labeled data. When the target data are fully unlabeled, our predictions rely solely on the source distribution, whereas partial target labels, when available, are integrated to improve efficiency. To address the challenges of data non-exchangeability and distribution non-identifiability, we identify the likelihood ratio by matching the covariate distributions of the source and target domains within a finite B-spline space. To accommodate complex error structures such as asymmetry and multimodality, our method constructs highest predictive density sets using a novel weight-adjusted conditional density estimator. This estimator models the source conditional density along a quantile process and transforms it, through appropriate weighting adjustments, to approximate the target conditional density. We establish the theoretical properties of the proposed method and evaluate its finite-sample performance through simulation studies and a real-data application to the MIMIC-III clinical database.
item.dc:creator: Menghan Yi, Yanlin Tang, Huixia Judy Wang

item.title: Individualized Prediction Bands in Causal Inference with Continuous Treatments
item.description: arXiv:2511.15075v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Individualized treatments are crucial for optimal decision-making and treatment allocation, specifically in personalized medicine based on the estimation of an individual's dose-response curve across a continuum of treatment levels, e.g., drug dosage. Current works focus on conditional mean and median estimates, which are useful but do not provide the full picture. We propose viewing causal inference with a continuous treatment as a covariate shift. This allows us to leverage existing weighted conformal prediction methods with both quantile and point estimates to compute individualized uncertainty quantification for dose-response curves. When used with quantile regression, our method, individualized prediction bands (IPB), enjoys a doubly robust coverage property. We demonstrate IPB via simulations and a real data analysis that assesses the additional medical expenditure caused by continued smoking for selected individuals. Our results show that IPB provides an effective solution to a gap in the individual dose-response uncertainty quantification literature.
item.dc:creator: Max Sampson, Kung-Sik Chan

item.title: Convex Mixed-Integer Programming for Causal Additive Models with Optimization and Statistical Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2511.21126v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of learning a directed acyclic graph from data generated by an additive, nonlinear structural equation model with Gaussian noise. We represent each nonlinear function through a basis expansion and derive a maximum likelihood estimator with group l0 regularization on the graph edges and l2 regularization on their strengths, with extensions to accommodate interaction effects. A key computational contribution is a scalable mixed-integer formulation that projects out the continuous model parameters, yields a convex objective in the remaining variables, and enables a tailored cutting-plane algorithm that is guaranteed to return a solution with a prespecified optimality gap. Our formulation can also incorporate background knowledge, including known edge presence or absence and partial ordering constraints. We establish consistency for graph recovery when the number of variables grows with the sample size. By linking optimization guarantees to statistical error bounds, we further derive an early stopping criterion in the cutting-plane algorithm that preserves consistency. Compared with existing approaches that assume equal error variances, restrict attention to linear structural equation models, or rely on heuristics, our method provides both optimization and statistical guarantees. Extensive simulations and two real-data analyses show markedly improved graph recovery.
item.dc:creator: Xiaozhu Zhang, Nir Keret, Rahul Mazumder, Ali Shojaie, Armeen Taeb

item.title: Vaccine sieve analysis on deep sequencing data using competing risks Cox regression with failure type subject to misclassification
item.description: arXiv:2512.09262v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how vaccines perform against different pathogen genotypes is crucial for developing effective prevention strategies, particularly for highly genetically diverse pathogens like HIV. Sieve analysis is a statistical framework used to determine whether a vaccine selectively prevents infection by certain genotypes while allowing breakthrough of other genotypes that evade immune responses. Traditionally, these analyses are conducted with a single sequence available per individual acquiring the pathogen. However, modern sequencing technology can provide detailed characterization of intra-individual viral diversity by capturing up to hundreds of pathogen sequences per person. In this work, we introduce methodology that extends sieve analysis to account for intra-individual viral diversity. Our approach estimates vaccine efficacy against viral populations with at least a small threshold of vaccine-mismatched mutations. To account for differential resolution of information from differing sequence counts per person, we use competing risks Cox regression with modeled causes of failure and propose an empirical Bayes approach for the classification model. Simulation studies demonstrate that our approach reduces bias, provides nominal confidence interval coverage, and improves statistical power compared to conventional methods. We apply our method to the HVTN 705 Imbokodo trial, which assessed the efficacy of a heterologous vaccine regimen in preventing HIV-1 infection.
item.dc:creator: James Peng, Michal Juraska, Pamela A. Shaw, Peter B. Gilbert

item.title: On estimands in sequential target trial emulation
item.description: arXiv:2601.03377v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The target trial framework enables causal inference from longitudinal observational data by emulating randomized trials initiated at multiple time points. Standard analyses typically pool information across trials via parametric models, defining the causal estimand implicitly as a regression coefficient. However, this practice presents several issues: it makes the target effect dependent on the estimation strategy; it obscures interpretation when noncollapsible estimands are used; it does not reflect a clear target population when pooling across heterogeneous trials. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an estimand-first strategy for sequential target trial emulation, centered around the choice of model-free estimands, rather than model specification. This ensures that treatment effects remain clearly interpretable for well-defined populations even under model misspecification. We propose estimands suitable for different study designs, and develop accompanying G-computation and inverse probability weighted estimators. Applications on simulations and real data on antimicrobial de-escalation in an intensive care unit setting demonstrate the greater clarity and reliability of the proposed methodology over traditional techniques.
item.dc:creator: Edoardo Efrem Gervasoni, Liesbet De Bus, Stijn Vansteelandt, Oliver Dukes

item.title: Quadruply robust methods for causal mediation analysis
item.description: arXiv:2601.22592v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Estimating natural effects is a core task in causal mediation analysis. Existing triply robust (TR) frameworks (Tchetgen Tchetgen & Shpitser 2012) and their extensions have been developed to estimate the natural effects. In this work, we introduce a new quadruply robust (QR) framework that enlarges the model class for unbiased identification. We study two modeling strategies. The first is a nonparametric modeling approach, under which we propose a general QR estimator that supports the use of machine learning methods for nuisance estimation. We also study high-dimensional settings, where the dimensions of covariates and mediators may both be large. In these settings, we adopt a parametric modeling strategy and develop a model quadruply robust (MQR) estimator to limit the impact of model misspecification. Simulation studies and a real data application demonstrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Zhen Qi, Yuqian Zhang

item.title: Conformal prediction for high-dimensional functional time series: Applications to subnational mortality
item.description: arXiv:2603.10674v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In statistics, forecast uncertainty is often quantified using a specified statistical model, though such approaches may be vulnerable to model misspecification, selection bias, and limited finite-sample validity. While bootstrap procedures may alleviate some of these concerns, their validity is not guaranteed and they are often computationally demanding. Instead, we take a model-agnostic and distribution-free approach, namely conformal prediction, to construct pointwise prediction intervals in high-dimensional functional time series. Among a rich family of conformal prediction methods, we study split, non-conformity score, sequential predictive, and adaptive conformal prediction. In split and non-conformity score conformal prediction, the data are divided into training, validation, and test sets, and the interval width is calibrated on the validation set so that the empirical coverage probability matches the nominal level, by tuning a coefficient of the residual standard deviation and by taking an empirical quantile of the non-conformity scores, respectively. Sequential predictive conformal prediction removes the need for a validation set by updating predictive quantiles sequentially via an autoregressive process, whereas adaptive conformal prediction updates the significance level over time according to the coverage of past intervals. Using subnational age- and sex-specific $\log$ mortality data from Japan and Canada, we compare the finite-sample forecast performance of the conformal prediction methods considered, using empirical coverage probability and the mean interval score.
item.dc:creator: Han Lin Shang, Chang Liu

item.title: Amortized Inference for Correlated Discrete Choice Models via Equivariant Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2603.24705v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Discrete choice models are fundamental tools in management science, economics, and marketing. Logit models dominate applied work because they yield closed-form choice probabilities, but IID Gumbel errors impose restrictive substitution patterns. We propose an amortized inference approach based on a neural network emulator that approximates choice probabilities under general, potentially correlated, error distributions. We develop a specialized neural network architecture respecting the invariance properties of discrete choice models and provide group-theoretic foundations for universal approximation from a minimal set of invariant features. Using Sobolev training, the emulator learns choice probabilities and their derivatives, enabling rapid likelihood and gradient evaluation. We show that emulator-based maximum likelihood estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal under mild approximation conditions. Simulations show substantial gains over the GHK simulator in accuracy and speed. Using NielsenIQ data on household laundry-detergent purchases, we estimate correlated-probit and correlated-Gumbel models with rich household-level random effects. The IID period-error restriction---and hence the conditional-IIA restriction underlying conventional mixed logit---is strongly rejected. The Bayesian information criterion (BIC) selects a correlated-Gumbel model with a three-factor period-error covariance structure. We find that allowing correlated period errors materially changes predicted product substitution patterns.
item.dc:creator: Easton Huch, Michael Keane

item.title: Reconciling Latent Variables and Networks: Exploring and extending the Psychometric-Toolbox
item.description: arXiv:2603.26116v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Since the introduction of network psychometrics, several connections to statistical models in "classical" psychometrics (i.e., Factor Analysis, Structural Equation Modeling, Item Response Theory) as well as to approaches from other research fields have been established. This paper reviews, synthesizes, and extends these developments, presenting them in an accessible visual format. This perspective opens up promising opportunities to extend the psychometric-toolbox by incorporating and learning from statistical methodologies developed in other areas of research, which often address similar or even identical problems. Highlighting these methodological commonalities may also foster collaboration across research fields that have traditionally remained largely independent. Moreover, awareness of these connections may render methodological development more systematic and goal-directed and may enable a meaningful division of labor, for example between the development of statistical methodology and its practical implementation for empirical research through software tools. Finally, these methodological advances provide new opportunities for empirical research and may contribute to a reconciliation with longstanding conceptual issues concerning psychometric constructs and, more broadly, psychological phenomena.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Kistermann, Maarten Marsman, Vivato V. Andriamiarana, Augustin Kelava

item.title: A CV-TMLE global test approach to improve power in rare disease clinical studies with multiple-component endpoints
item.description: arXiv:2605.02851v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rare disease trials face unique statistical challenges due to limited patient populations and heterogeneous clinical manifestations among patients. Multiple endpoints are often necessary to comprehensively capture treatment benefits. A global test is an approach for evaluating whether a treatment has any beneficial effect across multiple endpoints. We propose a new global test based on a weighted composite endpoint. The proposed global test employs shrinkage-based cross-validated targeted maximum likelihood estimation (CV-TMLE) to learn data-adaptive weights that maximize power while maintaining Type I error control. Shrinkage can be tailored to incorporate existing domain knowledge, such as anticipated relative effect sizes. In simulation studies designed to reflect real rare disease trial settings, the proposed procedure demonstrated improved power over standard multiplicity adjustments and classical global tests (such as the O'Brien test), while maintaining nominal Type I error, when effects are heterogeneous across endpoints. The proposed method simultaneously learns an optimal weighted composite outcome and provides an unbiased and efficient targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE) for the average treatment effect (ATE) on that weighted outcome, with valid inference taking into account that the ATE is data dependent.
item.dc:creator: Tianyue Zhou, Susan Gruber, Hana Lee, Wonyul Lee, Lei Nie, Mark van der Laan

item.title: Pseudo-Likelihood Regression for the Marginal Rate of Recurrent Events with a Competing Terminal Event
item.description: arXiv:2605.25934v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Regression modeling of recurrent and terminal events continues to present methodological challenges in survival analysis. Existing approaches either make unverifiable assumptions about the dependence between the two event types, rely on a proportional mean rate assumption, or use ad hoc estimating equations. We propose a semiparametric regression model based on a novel weighted pseudo-likelihood function that directly targets the marginal rate of the recurrent event and extends the Ghosh--Lin model to a large class of transformation models. Our framework accommodates external time-dependent covariate effects on the marginal rate and enables flexible prediction of the marginal mean. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimators and propose a robust sandwich estimator for the variance. In simulation studies, we demonstrate a strong performance of the proposed estimator under independent right-censoring. We apply the method to data from the interim analysis of a randomized clinical trial on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to predict the expected number of severe exacerbations, and illustrate how the choice of regression model affects the estimated covariate effects and predictions.
item.dc:creator: Anna Bellach, Michael R. Kosorok

item.title: Hierarchical Bayesian Estimation of Covariance Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2606.24751v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework for covariance matrix estimation built on a key observation: while equivariance under the full general linear group GL(p) is well known, it is an extremely restrictive property. Estimators equivariant to GL(p) are limited to scalar multiples of the sample covariance matrix and carry considerably larger risks than shrinkage estimators. By contrast, commonly used shrinkage estimators, including the Haff empirical Bayes estimator and the Ledoit-Wolf estimators, are all equivariant under the smaller orthogonal group O(p). Exploiting this structure, we establish that the Haar measure Bayes rule in an oracle eigenvalue model is the minimum risk estimator within the class of O(p)-equivariant estimators, and derive oracle Bayes rules for the covariance and precision matrices under the squared Frobenius, Stein, and squared Stein loss functions. These oracle rules serve as theoretical benchmarks for all O(p)-equivariant estimators. To approximate them when the true eigenvalues are unknown, we introduce a hierarchical Bayes model that places a finite P\'olya tree prior on the eigenvalue distribution and uses Gibbs sampling to generate posterior draws, yielding both shrinkage estimates for the eigenvalues and approximations to the oracle Bayes rules. In simulations, the resulting estimators come close to the risk of the oracle rules and have smaller risk than commonly used estimators, particularly when p/n is large. In an application to monthly returns of 49 US industry portfolios, the proposed estimators had the highest out-of-sample likelihood of all the estimators we compared, and their minimum-variance portfolios had variance comparable to that of estimators designed specifically for portfolio selection.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Yekutieli, Daniel Xiang, Jonas Wallin, Malgorzata Bogdan

item.title: Bayesian Distilled Clustering for High-Dimensional Mixture Models
item.description: arXiv:2608.06509v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Latent subgroup analysis is central to fields such as genomics, precision medicine, and social science, where the goal is to identify heterogeneous populations with distinct covariate structures or response behaviors. Mixture models provide a natural probabilistic framework for this task, representing the data-generating distribution as a weighted combination of subgroup-specific laws with unobserved labels. In high-dimensional regimes, these analyses face significant challenges. Often, only a small subset of covariates drives meaningful subgroup separation; the remaining variables may introduce noise or redundancy. Standard clustering methods typically treat all dimensions as equal, but in high-dimensional spaces, irrelevant coordinates can distort distances and obscure the low-dimensional structures defining latent classes. This paper introduces a Bayesian distilled clustering framework for high-dimensional mixture models. We propose that clustering should occur within a statistically justified subspace rather than the full ambient space. Our method utilizes a Bayesian variable selection model to estimate posterior inclusion probabilities, quantifying the evidence that each covariate contributes to subgroup separation or response behavior. A "distilled" covariate set is then identified by controlling the expected false-discovery proportion. Clustering is performed on this reduced subspace, followed by conditional independence diagnostics to examine subgroup-specific dependencies among selected variables. Critically, this framework is model-based: the distillation step is tied directly to the mixture structure and response model rather than a generic dimension-reduction criterion. This ensures the resulting subspace remains aligned with the scientific objective: identifying latent subgroups that differ in both distributional structure and behavior.
item.dc:creator: Pulkita Aggarwal (Abstract Math Institute), Abhishek Bhattacharjee (Abstract Math Institute)

item.title: A Two Stage Quasi-Likelihood Estimation Method for High Dimensional Generalized Structural Equation Models
item.description: arXiv:2608.16017v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Estimating high dimensional Generalized Structural Equation Models presents severe computational challenges. Traditional simultaneous estimators frequently suffer from numerical instability and prohibitive computational costs. Moreover, there are no tractable algorithms for families such as Poisson, negative binomial, and gamma. To overcome these limitations, this article introduces a Two Stage Quasi-Likelihood Expectation-Maximization framework. The proposed method isolates the structural model from the measurement model. First, it approximates the conditional distribution of the latent variables given the observed indicators. Second, it employs marginal quasi-likelihood estimating equations to evaluate the structural parameters, deriving the necessary conditional moments either exactly or through Monte Carlo integration. This approach completely avoids the need to evaluate the full joint likelihood. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our method drastically reduces computational runtime, providing a numerically stable framework that minimizes the mean squared error and structural bias to yield a scalable and flexible solution for analyzing complex latent variable models.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad W. Hattab

item.title: Faster Estimates from Binned Test Scores---With Discussion of Normality, Bias, and Reliability
item.description: arXiv:2609.36312v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Education agencies often summarize test score distributions by counting how many students scored in 3 to 5 bins. Means and standard deviations (SDs) can be estimated from bin counts using a HETOP model, which assumes that scores are normally distributed within each school or district. However, most HETOP software takes minutes to hours if the number of schools or districts is large. We present a fast HETOP algorithm that produces HETOP estimates in less than a millisecond per district. The algorithm is implemented in the fast_hetop function of the binest package for RL: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/binest/refman/binest.html#topic+fast_hetop HETOP estimates of the mean are highly reliable; estimates of the SD are not as good. Maximum likelihood estimates are generally excellent but can be biased and unreliable if scores are not normal or scores are concentrated in the top or bottom bin. Empirical Bayes shrinkage improves unreliable estimates. Standard errors are smaller if the data represents the whole population of students rather than a sample. HETOP estimates are usable for many purposes, but it would be better if education agencies reported means and SDs directly.
item.dc:creator: Paul T. von Hippel

item.title: An Integrated Framework for Rule-Based Data Editing
item.description: arXiv:2610.16947v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Statistical data editing must restore consistency while limiting changes to observed data. This paper links questionnaire routing, semantic edits, diagnosis, and correction verification through a common specification. The framework applies to dependencies admitting a normalized acyclic routing representation. Routing metadata generate Horn clauses requiring selected questions to be answered and skipped questions to remain blank. Together with supplied semantic edits and explicit domain and auxiliary conditions, these requirements characterize admissibility without generating all implied rules. Indexed requirements link violations to their sources and identify inputs whose modification can affect them. A weighted violation count guides correction: with complete checks and positive weights, it is zero exactly for admissible records. Returned corrections can therefore be verified independently of the search procedure. Minimum modification cost is addressed separately through sufficient conditions for a combined penalty objective and certificates obtained when an output attains a valid cost lower bound. A real household survey application illustrates a practical use of the proposed framework. The workflow supports traceable consistency restoration; the statistical accuracy of replacement values and their effects on survey estimates require separate assessment.
item.dc:creator: Pierpaolo Massoli

item.title: Fr\'echet Kriging for Metric Space-Valued Spatial Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.32979v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Spatial prediction of non-Euclidean data, such as probability distributions, symmetric positive semidefinite matrices, and networks, arises in many modern applications. Such data are naturally modeled as elements of general metric spaces, where classical kriging methods that rely on vector space structure are no longer directly applicable. We introduce Fr\'echet kriging, a general framework for spatial prediction of metric space-valued data. Fr\'echet kriging replaces the weighted average in classical ordinary kriging with a weighted Fr\'echet mean, while the weights are determined by characterizing the spatial dependence structure through a generalized variogram. This construction allows the proposed method to preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space without requiring an embedding into a linear space. We establish theoretical properties of the proposed predictor, including a surrogate optimality property and consistency under variogram misspecification. Simulation studies for univariate distributions and symmetric positive semidefinite matrices demonstrate favorable predictive performance compared with existing approaches. We further illustrate the practical utility of the proposed framework through applications to joint probability densities of daily minimum and maximum temperatures and inter-industry monetary flow networks.
item.dc:creator: Ryo Okano, Daisuke Kurisu, Hans-Georg M\"uller

item.title: Distribution-free predictive inference with instrumental variables
item.description: arXiv:2610.35605v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of predictive inference with outcomes missing not at random, when instrumental variables are available. While conformal prediction and weighted conformal prediction provide valid distribution-free inference when outcomes are missing completely at random and missing at random, respectively, inference is generally not possible without additional assumptions when outcomes are missing not at random. In this work, we consider a setting where we remain within the distribution-free framework but instead have access to an instrumental variable (IV). We explore the theoretical possibility of IV predictive inference and establish that it is characterized by a parameter that we refer to as the identification index. We derive an impossibility result for the case where the identification index is not sufficiently large, showing that any distribution-free approach fails to provide informative inference in this case. For the case where the identification index is sufficiently large, we introduce a practical method that achieves informative predictive inference. Our method leverages modern semiparametric efficiency theory which involves deriving the efficient influence function of the identifying functional for sharp IV bounds of the quantiles of the missing outcome, delivering a double robustness property in the coverage guarantee of the proposed framework for IV-based predictive inference. We illustrate the theoretical results and the performance of the proposed procedure through simulations and two real-data applications---FES wages and NHANES III self-reported heights.
item.dc:creator: Yonghoon Lee, Edgar Dobriban, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen

item.title: Improving Efficiency and Power in Small Rare-Disease Trials Through Prespecified, Data-Adaptive Covariate Adjustment
item.description: arXiv:2611.15071v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Covariate adjustment can potentially improve efficiency in randomized clinical trials, but in rare diseases, limited prior knowledge makes it difficult to specify an adjustment at the design stage. Targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) with the Super Learner (TMLE+SL) can outperform fixed adjustment methods, such as the G-computation estimator, by leveraging machine learning to learn both the covariates and the functional form of the adjustment from the trial data. Estimating the known treatment mechanism can improve efficiency further. In simulations reflecting real rare-disease trials, TMLE+SL yielded valid inference and achieved greater efficiency and power than conventional analyses. Finally, we also provide practical guidance on specifying TMLE+SL in rare-disease trials.
item.dc:creator: Tianyue Zhou, Susan Gruber, Hana Lee, Wonyul Lee, Lei Nie, Mark van der Laan

item.title: Fold Weighting for Cross-Validation Under Continuous Distributional Drift
item.description: arXiv:2611.23184v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cross-validation weights all folds equally, so under drift the oldest folds count as much as the newest. We model drift by a H\"older condition in total variation distance and give finite-sample bounds on the excess deployment risk of the configuration that sliding-window cross-validation selects. Each bound splits into drift, estimation, and validation-noise terms. With equal weights the drift terms saturate as the record grows. With fold weights fixed in advance, the drift terms become weighted averages, which shrink as weight moves toward deployment. The noise term grows as the weights concentrate and shrinks with the batch size. The drift terms are linear in the weights and the noise term is convex, so minimizing the bound over the weights is a convex problem. Applications to U.S. earnings and flight delays show both sides of this trade-off. Weight on recent folds pays off when a change in the best predictor persists and each period has many observations, and equal weights do best when changes are short-lived.
item.dc:creator: Yegor Baranovski

item.title: Is It Worth Collecting Additional Covariates?
item.description: arXiv:2611.24031v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In many studies, basic covariates are routinely recorded at negligible cost, whereas acquiring additional covariates requires expensive or time-consuming procedures. Thus, a natural question is whether it is worth to collecting these additional covariates. Using the reduction in prediction interval width as criterion, we evaluate and test the gain brought by the additional covariates and hence answer this question. We consider the gain both marginally and conditionally on the observable characteristics. The conditional formulation captures subpopulation heterogeneity and supports individualized data acquisition decisions. To avoid restrictive parametric assumptions, we adopt a model-free framework that accommodates flexible nonparametric or machine learning methods. We propose an efficient influence function based method, with proven theoretical properties to achieve our purpose under mild nuisance convergence rates. Interestingly, we find the natural conformal prediction based method cannot achieve the same purpose: It fails in the marginal case and imposes much more stringent or even infeasible requirement on the nuisance parameter estimation procedures. We demonstrate the superior finite-sample performance of the proposed procedures through simulations and real data applications.
item.dc:creator: Wen Zhang, Yanyuan Ma, Liping Zhu

item.title: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves
item.description: arXiv:2611.26410v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow networks whose hidden-layer parameters are randomly generated and then kept fixed, while only the output coefficients are estimated. Conditional on the sampled parameters, RWNN regression is a linear sieve problem with random approximation space. We show that such random sieves cannot remain uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows. For parametrized feature families satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population covariance matrix are proven to have polynomial upper bounds determined by the covering geometry of the parameter space, leading to a vanishing smallest eigenvalue. We develop approximation, estimation, and inference theory that explicitly treats the ill-conditioning. Under a $\beta$-H\"older source condition, we obtain both faster-than-Monte-Carlo $L^2$ approximation rates and new $L^\infty$ approximation bounds based on stratified sampling. We then derive improved consistency guarantees for ridge-regularized least squares driven by ridge effective dimension, spectral, and leverage-based stability conditions. For inference, we establish asymptotic linearity and Gaussian limits for linear functional directions while allowing the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix to vanish. Nondegeneracy is directional: we characterize it with a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient and extend it to smooth functionals via Riesz representation. Consistency of ridge-adjusted variance estimators is proved, yielding feasible studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate the deterioration of random-feature conditioning and the finite-sample behavior of the resulting estimation and inference procedures.
item.dc:creator: Giovanni Ballarin, Lukas Gonon, Lyudmila Grigoryeva

item.title: Inferring behind-the-meter demand components from net load via inverse optimization
item.description: arXiv:2410.02774v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding and forecasting electricity demand responses to price signals is essential to support the operational decisions of system operators, retailers, and regulators. Traditional time series and machine learning approaches have performed well under stable consumption patterns. However, the rise of active consumers with flexible assets, such as solar-plus-storage systems and electric vehicles, introduces new complexities. These consumers exhibit behind-the-meter behavior that is generally unobservable to system operators and retailers, who can typically only measure net demand at the boundary meters which are located at the connection points to the grid. Net demand reflects the aggregate of baseload consumption, flexible load shifting, and self-generation, all of which may respond nonlinearly to market prices. As these unobservable components grow, existing forecasting models may fail to capture the true dynamics of consumer behavior. This work develops and implements a data-driven inverse optimization framework to reveal behind-the-meter consumption patterns using only net demand data. By analyzing net demand as revealed at the grid connection point, we estimate parameters for a latent optimization model, enabling predictions that infer the unobservable components. This enables more accurate point and probabilistic forecasting of electricity demand under varying price signals. Thus, it provides actionable insights for system operators to improve local congestion management and flexibility extraction, as well as for retailers and aggregators, who could thereby optimize operations and tariffs to leverage consumer flexibility. We validate the methodology using real-world data, demonstrating improved forecasting accuracy over leading machine learning and time-series benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Adrian Esteban-Perez, Derek Bunn, Yashar Ghiassi-Farrokhfal

item.title: Econometric vs. Causal structure learning for time-series data: Implications for policy interventions using COVID-19 data
item.description: arXiv:2603.00041v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This study compares regression-based and causal structure-learning approaches to recovering temporal dependencies in UK COVID-19 data and assesses their suitability for policy analysis. We evaluate four econometric methods and eleven structure-learning algorithms using a common lag-expanded dataset that permits edges only from past to current variables. The dataset comprises 866 daily observations and 45 variables, represented by 55 numeric series after categorical encoding. Maximum lags of 1, 7, 14, 17 and 21 days are examined; all four econometric methods and ten structure-learning algorithms successfully return structures at every lag specification. We compare graph structure, complexity, fit and temporal-edge stability across lag specifications. The resulting graphs vary substantially in density, complexity, fit and stability. Agreement with the knowledge graph is limited, while low structural Hamming distance sometimes reflects sparsity rather than recovery of known relationships. Edge recurrence also varies markedly by method, revealing sensitivity to the allowed history window. Diagnostics for VAR models using all lagged predictors indicate residual dependence, non-normality and instability; estimation becomes infeasible at longer lag orders. Policy evaluation raises further concerns: few mobility-to-infection links emerge, few meet the empirical coverage criterion, and none do so in longer-lag analyses. Common temporal constraints therefore do not resolve methodological disagreement. Learnt dependency structures should not be treated as policy-ready causal models without stronger identification assumptions, robustness checks and sufficient empirical support for the interventions assessed.
item.dc:creator: Bruno Petrungaro, Anthony C. Constantinou

item.title: Rate-Optimal Randomised Kernel Quadrature
item.description: arXiv:2605.18134v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Kernel quadrature is used to approximate integrals of smooth functions, with the worst-case error typically decaying at the minimax rate $n^{-\alpha/d}$ for smoothness $\alpha$ in dimension $d$. Existing rate-optimal methods often depend on deterministic point sets, sometimes tailored to a specific kernel. Here, we study randomised designs for kernel quadrature on compact and unbounded domains for kernels whose reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces are norm-equivalent to Sobolev spaces of integer order $\alpha>d/2$. We bound the worst-case error of prescribed designs adapted to a sampling density $p$ by $n^{-\alpha/d}$ times an explicit functional of the sampling and integration densities. Minimising this factor gives $p^\star\propto\pi^\gamma$ with $\gamma=2d/(2\alpha+d)$, where $\pi$ is the integration density. The proposal depends on the kernel only through its Sobolev order $\alpha$. Under local mass and cell-average conditions, together with a tail condition on $\mathbb{R}^d$, independent samples from $p^\star$ attain the same minimax rate with high probability, up to a logarithmic factor. The same bound also controls posterior contraction. We verify these conditions for Beta-type densities on the cube and, for integrands in $\mathcal{H}^\alpha(\mathbb{R}^d)$, for Gaussian and Student-$t$ measures. The deterministic minimax exponent for Student targets is $\min(\alpha,\nu+d/2)/d$, with a logarithmic gap between the bounds at $\alpha=\nu+d/2$.
item.dc:creator: Edoardo Bandoni (CEREMADE), Christian Robert (CEREMADE), Julien Stoehr (CEREMADE)

item.title: Event-Time Confounding Under Bursty Human Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2608.21294v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Web studies often measure what happens after a user action, such as a search after a chatbot answer. To credit an AI answer with later commercial activity, a study must separate what the answer caused from what the user would have done anyway. But people act in the middle of activity already underway, so the activity that drives what follows also chooses when the clock starts. We call this endogenous time zero. Using an opt-in panel that links conversational-AI use, browsing, and search, we insert inert timestamps (moments that match recent activity but mark no event) and rerun the standard analysis. In a pre-registered replication, these timestamps, which by construction cannot cause anything, reproduce 76% of the search increase after AI responses that follow recent browsing. Other users matched on 30-day activity, the usual control, give the same answer, and inert timestamps show a similar search excess across 16 kinds of Web events. Comparing with moments of matching recent history removes most of the increase, but no placebo audit we ran could confirm that this comparison is unbiased, and published studies almost never run one. We give a protocol for choosing comparisons and stress-testing estimators.
item.dc:creator: Michael Iannelli, Alan Ai

item.title: A complete characterization of sequential testability and change detectability in i.i.d. models
item.description: arXiv:2609.05752v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give qualitative and quantitative necessary and sufficient conditions for sequential testing and change detection in an i.i.d. composite problem. A level-\(\alpha\) test with power one against every alternative exists if and only if the alternatives are separated from the null by a countable family of finite-block events. Equivalent conditions use randomized tests, bounded scores, e-processes, reduced-filtration test supermartingales, and a countable cover with positive finite-block weak-$*$ convex-hull separation. The construction gives pointwise expected sample size \(O_Q(\log(1/\alpha))\). Quantitatively, one e-process attains the intrinsic pointwise growth rate \(\Gamma(Q)\) at every alternative if and only if a countable family of bounded block bets recovers these rates. The same condition characterizes simultaneous attainment of the sharp expected-sample-size coefficient \(1/\Gamma(Q)\); arbitrary attainable lower rate profiles admit an analogous characterization. Total-variation separability of the alternatives suffices for recovery. Weak lower semicontinuity of the KL projection, in particular weak compactness of the null, also identifies \(\Gamma(Q)\) with \(\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathrm{KL}(Q\|P)\). The qualitative and quantitative conditions also characterize change detectability under fixed-time false-alarm bounds \(\Prob_{P^\infty}(T_\gamma\le n)\le n/\gamma\), together with ordinary ARL control. Whenever countable rate recovery holds, for any \(\eta>0\) one calibrated e-detector has robust Lorden delay asymptotic to \((\log\gamma)/\Gamma(Q)\) at finite positive rates, while satisfying the stronger optional-horizon inequality and placing every null ARL in \([\gamma,(1+\eta)\gamma+1]\). Examples exhibit a strict cost of simultaneous optimality and show that ordinary ARL alone supports neither characterization, even with finite, tightly calibrated null means.
item.dc:creator: Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Doubly robust estimation of direct and spillover effects using multiple pre-treatment periods
item.description: arXiv:2610.37049v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. Under certain identifying assumptions, both components may be identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, even in the absence of an uncontaminated comparison group. Under a no-anticipation assumption, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time-series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment, provided that the model used for the extrapolation is correctly specified. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for possibly high-dimensional covariates by machine learning. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ consistent behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors under specific regularity conditions. We apply the framework to the compulsory licensing of enemy-owned patents in the United States in 1919. Licensing raised patenting in the licensed subclasses and in technologically close ones alike, so that a comparison-group design understates the total effect.
