item.title: Counting Under Disagreement: Dollar-Weighted Measurement, Selective Machine Labelling and Budgeted Human Review from Disagreeing AI Readers of Administrative Text
item.description: arXiv:2611.13215v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study AI-assisted measurement when one text label applies to many administrative records, the target is a monetary total, and the human readings that anchor the machines disagree. The testbed is 121,070 grant-purpose texts from US tax filings (799,675 records, $126.4B), labelled by a rule-based classifier and three language models, with a designed sample of 651 texts read independently by three people under one codebook, who then adjudicated the 152 texts they split on. We state exact conditions for a fixed-predictor difference estimator and for a cross-fitted predictor whose folds are assigned to the whole frame independently of the sample, under Poisson sampling, and assess the implemented fixed-size procedures by simulation: 8 predictors whose own totals span $12.5-15.0B agree to within $0.4B once rectified. Two rules that accept machine labels at a stated dollar-weighted error, weighted conformal p-values under a dollar measure and Learn-then-Test on the design estimate of the error, are evaluated on nested held-out folds and on design re-draws with synthetic truths; their error control in deployment is not established, and the count-based rule accepts no text under a dollar-drawn sample. In a replay that counts every reference label a policy queries, pilot included (not the readings behind it), a two-phase review policy whose calibrator is fitted on its own first phase reduces the RMSE of the total by 42% at 100 queries relative to dollar-proportional sampling, while pure Neyman allocation fails with an uncalibrated predictor. Independent readers shift the estimated total by $3.93B, 2.7 times the sampling interval; the adjudicated reading puts it at $13.49B; institution-level intervals under-cover at every size. Reference-dependent results are re-run under each reader. The results identify benefits and limits of using learned predictions to decide what a person should verify.

item.title: Does Increasing Government Spending on Tertiary Education Provide a Return on Investment? A Bayesian Causal Inference Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.18086v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Does public spending on tertiary (university) education generate a positive fiscal return once general economic growth is separated out? Cross-country data make this hard to answer because growing economies naturally collect more tax, international ratios divide per-student spending by GDP per person and student headcount, and cohorts take years to graduate. We assemble a five-year panel of 121 countries (1985-2024) and fit continuous-treatment Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests modelling four tax changes jointly whilst adjusting for starting conditions, predicted funding, and follow-up growth. A +10 percentage-point (pp) increase in per-student spending (% of GDP per person) shifts the tax mix toward direct income and profit taxation by +0.36 pp after 5 years (P = 0.93, posterior probability of a positive effect) and +0.71 pp after 10 years (P = 0.96). Overall tax-to-GDP takes a decade to respond: 10-year total non-resource tax rises by +0.24 pp of GDP (P = 0.89; +0.31 pp, P = 0.94 across four chains, retaining the conservative single-chain baseline) and direct income tax by +0.12 pp (P = 0.90; +0.15 pp, P = 0.93 across four chains) per +10 pp of per-student spending, by +0.37 pp (P > 0.99) after five-year within-country increases, and by +0.22 pp in total tax (P = 0.95) and +0.15 pp in direct income tax (P = 0.98) per +25% increase in real PPP dollars per student. Comparing one cohort's degree cost against its 40-year career taxes shows a typical three- to five-fold expected total tax return in high-income economies with wide intervals reflecting macro noise (EUR 2.4B in Ireland returning EUR 9.7B in total tax, 95% CI EUR -10B to +32B, net-profit probability 0.77, and EUR 2.9B in direct income tax; EUR 11.6B in the UK returning EUR 58B, 95% CI EUR -60B to +190B), whereas expanding the budget without protecting spending per student yields no return.
